sourceDefinition: Wide, or broad; (S, K;) as also ↓ muSaf~aHN , (K,) which latter is the more common; both applied in this sense to a sword, and to anything; and ↓ maSofuwHN signifies the same. (TA.) One says, wajohu h`*aA Als~ayofi muSofaHN The face of this sword is wide, or broad; from ↓ A^aSofaHotuhu . (S.) And Darabahu biAls~ayofi muSofaHFA , (S, A, K,) and ↓ maSofuwHFA , (IAar, TA,) and ↓ muSofiHFA , (A, [this last relating to the agent,]) He struck him with the breadth, or width, [or flat, ] of the sword; (S, A, K;) not with its edge: (A:) and Drbh bAlsyf gayora muSofaHK He struck him with the sword not with its breadth, but with its edge. (TA.) And rajulN Alr~aA^osi ↓ muSaf~aHu A man wide, or broad, in respect of the head; (S, TA;) and so muSofaHu Alr~aA^osi . (TA.) ― -b2- Also Having the two sides of his head depressed, and the side of the forehead prominent, (K, TA,) and the occiput also prominent and conspicuous: (TA:) or having the fore and hind parts of the head projecting. (AZ, Mgh.) ― -b3- And A head compressed in the parts next the temples, so as to be long between the forehead and the back of the neck. (K.) ― -b4- A nose straight in the bone; (K, TA;) having the bone even with the forehead. (TA.) ― -b5- And A smooth, or soft, or smooth and soft, and beautiful, face. (Lh, K.) ― -b6- Applied to a sword, (TA,) Inclined, or bent: (S, K, TA:) and inverted, or reversed: (Ibn-Buzurj, K, TA:) that is turned upon its edge when one strikes with it: and that is inclined, or bent, when one desires to sheath it. (TA.) ― -b7- It is said in a trad., qalobu Almuw^omini muSofaHN EalaY AlHaq~i , meaning (assumed tropical:) The heart of the believer is inclined to the truth; (S, L;) as though its side ( SafoHuhu i. e. jaAnibuhu ) were placed upon it. (L.) And muSofaHN applied to a heart signifies also (assumed tropical:) Turned away from the truth: (TA:) [or] so applied, in which are combined faith and hypocrisy: (K, TA:) or, accord. to Khálid, that falls short of its duty; in which is latent rancour, malevolence, malice, or spite; and which is not sincere in its religion: (Sh, TA:) or it means double-faced; one who meets the unbelievers with one face, and the believers with another face; SafoHN signifying the “ face, ” of anything. (IAth, TA.) -A2- And AlmuSofaHu is a name of The sixth of the arrows used in the game called Almayosir ; (S, K;) as also Almusobilu . (S.)

sourceDefinition: : see muSofaHN , in two places. ― -b2- [Hence,] muSaf~aHapN signifies A sword; as also ↓ muSaf~iHapN : (K: [but see what follows:]) accord. to IAar, muSaf~aHaAtN [its pl. (K)] signifies swords; because they are made broad, or wide, and lengthened out, in the forging: (S:) or, as some say, it signifies broad, or wide, swords. (TA. [See also SafiyHapN .]) Lebeed says, describing clouds, kaA^an~a muSaf~aHaAtK fiY *uraAhaA waA^anowaAHFA Ealayohin~a AlmaA=liY [ As though there were swords, or broad swords, upon their summits, and wailing women having upon them the pieces of rag which such women hold in wailing and with which they make signs ]: (S, TA:) Az says that he likens the lightning, in the darkness of the clouds, to broad swords: (TA:) and IAar says that mSf~HAt here means swords: but as some relate the verse, the word is ↓ muSaf~iHaAt [meaning women clapping their hands ]; as though he likened the clouds' discovering themselves when the lightning shone from them, and they opened, and then met together after the lightning's becoming extinct, to the clapping of women's hands: (S: in some copies of which, Algayov is put for Algayom :) or, accord. to this reading, he likens the sound of the thunder to women's clapping of their hands. (TA.) ― -b3- Also A she-camel (T, L) that is kept from being milked, in order that she may become fat. (T, L, K.)

A_iSomaAtN ; (K;) and ↓ Sm~t , inf. n. taSomiytN ; (S, K; but only the inf. n. is mentioned;) He was, or became, silent, mute, or speechless; syn. sakata : (S, A, Msb, K:) or he was, or became, long silent or mute or speechless: (M, Mgh:) but there is a difference between sakata and Samata ; for the former is said of him who has the power, or faculty, of speech, but abstains from making use of it; whereas the latter is sometimes said of that which has not the power, or faculty, of speech. (Er-Rághib, MF and TA in art. skt .) The Arabs say, (Ks, TA,) and it is said in a trad., (TA,) laA Samota yawomFA A_ilaY All~ayoli , or yawomN , or yawomK , i. e. There shall be no keeping silence a whole day [ until night ]. (Ks, K, TA. [In the “ Jámi' es-Sagheer, ” we find lA SumaAta instead of lA Samota : and El-Munáwee, in his Commentary on that work, says that the keeping silence for a whole day is forbidden by the words of this trad. because it is an imitation of a Christian custom.]) And A_i*onuhaA SumaAtuhaA [in another trad., relating to the asking a virgin if she consent to be married, lit. Her permission is her silence, ] means her silence is like her permission, i. e. it suffices. (Msb.) One says also, jaA='a bimaA SaA='a waSamata (assumed tropical:) [ He brought what was vocal and what was mute ]; maA SaA='a meaning sheep, or goats, and camels; and maA Samata , gold and silver: (IAar, TA:) SaA='a in this saying is formed by transposition from SaA^aY [q. v.]. (S in art. SA^Y .)

definition: Such a one is, or was, at the point of accomplishing the affair.
sourceDefinition: Such a one is, or was, at the point of accomplishing the affair. (S.) And A^anaA EalaY SimaAti HaAjatiY I am at the point of accomplishing my want. (M.) And baAta EalaY SimaAti A^amorihi He passed the night resolved upon his affair. (TA.) And huwa biSimaAtihi He is at the point of [ attaining ] his purpose: (M, TA:) Aboo-Málik says that SimaAtN signifies qaSodN [i. e. purpose, intention, &c.]. (TA.) And one says, baAta mina Alqawomi EalaY SimaAtK He passed the night in a place where he was seen and heard by the people, near to them. (S, TA.)

definition: Silent, mute, or speechless: (Msb:) pl.
sourceDefinition: Silent, mute, or speechless: (Msb:) pl. SaAmituwna (Kur vii. 192) [and SumuwtN , occurring in the K in art. zm ]. [Hence,] one says, maA lahu SaAmitN walaA naATiqN (tropical:) [ He has not mute nor vocal property; or he has not dead nor live stock ]: (S, M, A:) by the former are meant gold and silver; (S, M, Msb, K;) and by the latter, camels, (S, K,) and sheep or goats, (S,) or animals: (M:) i. e. he has not aught. (S.) ― -b2- Also, of camels, (assumed tropical:) Twenty, (O, K,) and the like. (O.) ― -b3- And of milk, (assumed tropical:) Such as is thick. (S, O, K.)

sourceDefinition: and bibalodapi A_iSomita AZ explains as meaning [ I met him, or met with him, or found him, ] in a desert place, in which was no one to cheer by his company: (S: [and in like manner the latter phrase is expl. in the M:]) accord. to Kr, bibalodapK A_iSomita ; but the phrase commonly known is bibalodapi A_iSomita : (M:) or tarakotuhu bibalodapi A_iSomita [ I left him ] in the desert, or waterless desert: or in such a place that it was not known where he was: (K:) and biSaHoraA='i A_iSomita (M, K) meaning as above, (K,) or having the latter of these two meanings: (M:) and biwaHo$i A_iSomita and ↓ A_iSomitapa , (M, K,) mentioned, but not expl., by Lh, (M,) meaning as above, (K,) or app. meaning in the desert, or waterless desert: (M:) and some say, biwaHo$i AlA_iSomitayoni : (TA:) ASmt is as above, with the disjunctive alif; and also with the conjunctive [i. e. A@Somita ]: (O, K:) it is imperfectly decl., (S, MF, TA,) because combining the quality of a proper name with the fem. gender or with the measure of a verb: (MF, TA:) it is said that the desert, or waterless desert, is thus called because in it one fears much; as though everyone [therein] said to his companion, ASmt [i. e. AuSomuto or A^aSomito , “ Be thou silent ”]; like as they say of a mahomah that it is so called because a man [therein] says to his companion, maho maho : (MA:) [for] accord. to some the word A_iSomit is an imperative changed into a subst., and hence the ' is disjunctive, and it may be with kesr accord. to a dial. var. [of the imperative] that has not reached us: accord. to Yákoot, it is the name of a particular desert; but others say that the proper name [of that desert] is waHo$u A_iSomita . (TA in art. wH$ .)

definition: [primarily signifies Made, or rendered, silent, mute, or speechless.
sourceDefinition: [primarily signifies Made, or rendered, silent, mute, or speechless. ― -b2- And hence,] Solid; not hollow; having no cavity. (A 'Obeyd, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K.) [For that which is without a cavity is generally non-sonorous.] ― -b3- And A door, (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) and a lock, (M, K,) closed, or locked, (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) so that one cannot find the way to open it. (S, M, * K. *) A poet says, wamino duwni layolaY muSomataAtu AlmaqaASiri [ And in the way to Leylà are what are closed, &c., of chambers to which the owner alone has access: maqaASir being used by poetic license for maqaASayr , pl. of maqoSuwrapN ]. (TA.) ― -b4- Also A garment, or piece of cloth, of one, unmixed, colour. (M, Mgh, K.) The garment thus termed that is disliked is That of which the warp and woof are both of silk: or such as is woven of undressed silk, and then dressed, and dyed of one colour: (Mgh:) [or] such as is termed muSomatN mino xaz~K , i. e. consisting entirely of silk, not mixed with cotton nor with other material, was forbidden by the Prophet. (TA.) ― -b5- [Hence,] farasN muSomatN A horse of one, unmixed, colour; in which is no colour differing from the rest: (S, A, TA:) pl. xayolN muSomataAtN . (TA.) And A^adohamu muSomatN [applied to a horse] (assumed tropical:) Black unmixed with any other colour. (TA.) ― -b6- [Hence also,] A_inaA='N muSomatN (assumed tropical:) A vessel not silvered, or not ornamented with silver. (Mgh.) And bayoDapN muSomatapN (assumed tropical:) A helmet made of one piece. (AO, TA in art. byD .) And HaloYN muSomatN (assumed tropical:) A woman's ornament that is not intermixed with another: or, accord. to Ahmad Ibn- 'Obeyd, that has stuck fast upon its wearer, so that it does not move about; such as the armlet, and the anklet, and the like. (TA.) ― -b7- The fahod [or lynx, an animal proverbial for much sleeping,] is said to be muSomtu Aln~awomi (tropical:) [app. meaning A heavy sleeper ]. (A, TA.) ― -b8- AlHuruwfu AlmuSomatapu are All the letters [ of the Arabic alphabet ] except those called Huruwfu Al*~alaAqapi [or AlHuruwfu Al*~uloqu ]; (M, TA;) i. e. (TA) all the letters except those comprised in the phrase muro binafolK . (K, TA.) [What is here rendered “ except ” (i. e. maA EadaA ) is said by MF to be omitted in most of the copies of the K.] ― -b9- See also muSam~ato .

The garment thus termed that is disliked is That of which the warp and woof are both of silk: or such as is woven of undressed silk, and then dressed, and dyed of one colour: (Mgh:) [or] such as is termed muSomatN mino xaz~K , i. e. consisting entirely of silk, not mixed with cotton nor with other material, was forbidden by the Prophet. (TA.)

[Hence,] farasN muSomatN A horse of one, unmixed, colour; in which is no colour differing from the rest: (S, A, TA:) pl. xayolN muSomataAtN . (TA.) And A^adohamu muSomatN [applied to a horse] (assumed tropical:) Black unmixed with any other colour. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , [aor. yaSuwlu ,] inf. n. SawolN and SawolapN (S, O, K) and SiyaAlN , (O,) He leaped, or sprang, upon him: (S, O, K:) and (K) SaAla Ealayohi , (M, K,) aor. yaSuwlu , (TA,) inf. n. SawolN and SiyaAlN and Suw^uwlN and SawalaAnN and SaAlN and maSaAlapN , he sprang, or rushed, upon him; made an assault, or attack, upon him; namely, his adversary, or antagonist; syn. saTaA ; (M, K, TA;) and Hamala : (TA:) [or he sprang upon him and seized him violently or laid violent hands upon him; for so saTaA is said to signify:] and SAl Ealayohi (tropical:) he overbore him, overpowered him, or subdued him; (S, * O, * Msb, * TA; [a meaning also assigned to saTaA ;]) namely, one man another nam. (TA.) [See also 1 in art. Syl .] One says, rub~a qawolK A^a$ad~u mino SawolK Many a saying is more severe than a leaping or springing [&c.]. (S, O.) And it is said in a trad. respecting prayer, bika A^aSuwlu , meaning [ By Thee may I ] spring, or rush, or assault, and subdue. (TA.) ― -b2- SAl , aor. as above, inf. n. SawolN , is also said of a stallion [camel], meaning He leaped, or sprang: or, accord. to AZ, SAl , inf. n. SawolN and SiyaAlN , said of a camel, means he leaped, or sprang, upon the [ other ] camels, and fought them: (Msb:) or one says of a stallion, SAl EalaY AlA_ibili , inf. n. SawolN , meaning he fought the [ other ] camels, (M, K,) and sent them on before: (M:) or, accord. to AZ, one says of a camel, (S,) or, accord. to Es-Sarakustee, some of the Arabs say of a camel, (Msb,) Saw^ula , (S, Msb, [in one of my copies of the S SAl , but the former is the right,]) like qaruba , (Msb,) with ' , (S, Msb,) inf. n. SaA^lapN , meaning he betook himself to the killing of men, and springing, or rushing, upon them: (S) and without ' in speaking of the act of one adversary, or antagonist, against another: (Msb:) Hamzeh El-Isbahánee says, in his “ Proverbs, ” that SAl Aljamalu means the camel bit; but he is alone in saying this. (TA.) One says also, SAl AlEayoru , meaning The he-ass attacked the she-ass: (S, O:) or SAl AlEayoru EalaY AlEaAnapi the heass drove away the she-ass, or the herd of wild she-asses, (M, K, TA,) and attacked her or them, biting her or them with the fore teeth, and kicking her or them with the hind leg or hind legs. (TA.) -A2- SAl Albur~a , aor. as above, inf. n. SawolN , He swept away, or cleared, the wheat from the pieces of stick and of rubbish: and AlHinoTapa ↓ Saw~alonaA we swept the wheat [ well, and so cleared it from rubbish ]: the teshdeed denotes intensiveness of meaning: (O:) ↓ Alt~aSowiylu [or taSowiylu Albayodari ] means the sweeping of the bayodar [or collected wheat or grain, or perhaps the place in which wheat or grain is trodden out ], (O,) or of the sides thereof ( nawaAHiY Albayodari [ to clear it of rubbish ]). (K.) -A3- Siyla : see art. Syl .

definition: A handful of herbs, (AHn, S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) mixed together, (S, A, Msb, K,) fresh and dry: (S, Msb, K:) or a handful of twigs of trees or shrubs;
sourceDefinition: A handful of herbs, (AHn, S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) mixed together, (S, A, Msb, K,) fresh and dry: (S, Msb, K:) or a handful of twigs of trees or shrubs; (Mgh, * Msb;) or of fruit-stalks of the raceme of a palm-tree: (Mgh, Msb:) originally, a number of twigs all having one root or stem: and afterwards applied to what is collected together: (Msb:) or a thing that one collects together, such as a bundle of [ the species of trefoil called ] raTobap ; and of what has a stem, and grows tall: (Fr, TA:) or whatever is collected together, and grasped with the hand: (AHeyth, TA:) or a bundle of herbs mixed together; or of firewood: pl. A^aDogaAvN . (TA.) In the Kur xxxviii. 43, it is said to mean A bundle of rushes ( A^asal , so in the Mgh and the O, in my copy of the Msb Avl [which I think a mistranscription, on account of what follows]), a hundred in number, (O, Msb,) consisting of slender stalks without leaves, (Mgh, Msb,) whereof mats are made. (Msb.) See also a prov. cited and expl. voce A_ilaAlapN . Hence, in a trad., DigovaAni mino naArK , meaning (tropical:) Two bundles of lighted firewood. (TA.) And, in another trad., minohumu AlA=xi*u AlD~igova , meaning (assumed tropical:) Among them is he who obtains somewhat of worldly goods. (TA.) ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) What is confused, and without truth, or reality, [of dreams, and] of news, or tidings, and of an affair. (Sh, TA.) A^aDogaAvu A^aHolaAmK , [occurring in the Kur xii. 44 and xxi. 5,] of which the sing. is Digovu HulomK , (Msb,) means (tropical:) Complications of dreams; (A;) or medleys of dreams, falsely resembling true dreams: (O, Msb:) or a dream of which the interpretation will not prove true, because of its confusedness: (ISh, S, K:) or a false dream; the pl. form being used to give emphasis to the meaning of unreality, or because the phrase comprehends various things: (Bd in xii. 44:) or A^aDogaAvu Alr~uw^oyaA means the terrors, or frightful things, of the dream. (Mujáhid, O, TA.) One says also, A^ataAnaA biA^aDogaAvK mina AlA^axobaAri , meaning (tropical:) He brought us [ various ] sorts of news, or tidings. (TA.) DigovN means also (assumed tropical:) A deed that is of a mixed kind, not pure, or not sincere. (IAth and O, from a trad.) And kalaAmN DigovN (assumed tropical:) Speech in which is no good: pl. A^aDogaAvN . (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, MA, K,) or AlmaAla , (Mgh, Msb,) inf. n. taDomiynN , (S,) He made him to be responsible, answerable, accountable, amenable, surety, or guarantee, (S, MA, Mgh, Msb, K,) for the thing, (S, MA, K,) or for the property. (Mgh, Msb.) [See an ex. in a verse cited voce muEab~adN .] ― -b2- Dam~anotu Al$~aYo'a ka*aA I made the thing to comprise, comprehend, or contain, such a thing. (Msb.) Hence, Dam~ana A@ll~`hu A^aSolaAba AlfuHuwli Aln~asola [ God has made the loins of the stallions to comprise, in the elemental state, the progeny ]. (Msb.) And Dm~nhu AlwiEaA='a He put it (i. e. anything) into the receptacle. (S, K.) And Dm~n Almay~ita Alqabora He deposited the dead body in the grave. (TA.) And Dm~n AlkitaAba ka*aA (assumed tropical:) He made the writing to comprise, or include, such a thing. (MA.) [And Dm~n AlkalaAma ka*aA (assumed tropical:) He made, or held, the sentence, or speech, or phrase, to imply such a thing. And Dm~n Alkalimapa maEonaY ka*aA (assumed tropical:) He made the word to imply or import, such a meaning. ] ― -b3- Alt~aDomiynu as a conventional term of those who treat of elegance of speech is (assumed tropical:) The making poetry to comprise a verse [ of another poet ]: (TA:) or the introducing into poetry a hemistich, or a verse, or two verses, of another poet, to complete the meaning intended, and for the purpose of corroborating the meaning, on the condition of notifying it as borrowed, beforehand, or of its being well known, so that the hearer will not imagine it to be stolen: and if it is a hemistich, or less than that, it is termed rafowN . (Har p. 267.) And as a conventional term of those who treat of versification, (assumed tropical:) The making a verse to be not complete otherwise than with what follows it. (TA.)

definition: and ↓ DamiynN One who is responsible, answerable, accountable, amenable, surety, or guarantee: (S, Msb, K:) both are mentioned by IAar as syn.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ DamiynN One who is responsible, answerable, accountable, amenable, surety, or guarantee: (S, Msb, K:) both are mentioned by IAar as syn., like saAminN and samiynN . (TA.) God is represented by the Prophet as saying, mano xaraja mujaAhidFA fiY sabiyliY waA@botigaA='i maroDaAtiY faA^anaA Ealayohi DaAminN wahuwa EalaY~a DaAminN , meaning [ Whoso goes forth as a warrior in my cause, and seeking, or seeking earnestly, to obtain my approval, ] I am responsible to him for what I have promised him, to recompense him living and dead; DAmn being made trans. by means of ElY because it implies the meaning of muHaAmK and raqiybN ; and the last clause means nearly the same, but is rendered as meaning and he is one who has [ a claim to ] responsibility on my part, as though care and mindfulness [of him] were obligatory on me. (Mgh.) And it is said in a trad., AlA_imaAmu DaAminN waAlmuw^a*~inu muw^otamanN : (Mgh, JM, * TA:) [the latter clause has been expl. in art. A^mn (voce A^amiynN ):] the former clause means, The imám [or leader of prayer ] is as though he were responsible for the correctness of the prayer of those who follow him: (JM, TA: [and the like is said, with other, similar, explanations, in the Mgh:]) or it means, the imám is careful, or mindful, for the people [ who follow him ], of [ the correctness of ] their prayer. (TA.) ― -b2- DaAminN and ↓ miDomaAnN applied to a she-camel, signify Having a fœtus in her belly: and the pls. are DawaAminu and maDaAmiynu . (IAar, L and TA in art. lqH and in the present art.) ― -b3- DaAminapN applied to rights, or dues, ( Huquwq ,) is used by Lebeed as meaning maDomuwnapN ; [see maDomuwnN ;] like as raAHilapN is used as meaning maroHuwlapN . (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [ A drum; ] a certain thing with which one beats, (S, O, K,) [or rather upon which one beats, ] well known, (Msb,) having a single face, and having two faces: (Msb, K:) pl. [of mult.] TubuwlN (O, Msb, K) and [of pauc.] A^aTobaAlN . (Msb, K.) [Hence] one says, huwa TabolN *uw wajohayoni [lit. He is a double-faced drum ]; meaning (tropical:) he is of ill-omened, or hard, aspect. (TA.) And fulaAnN yaDoribu AlT~abola taHota AlkisaA='i [lit. Such a one beats the drum beneath the garment called ksA' ; meaning, (assumed tropical:) strives to conceal what is notorious: similar to the Pers. saying Tabol daro ziyri Giliym zadano ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Also A raboEap [or small round basket, covered with leather, ] for perfumes. (TA.) And A sal~ap [or round basket ] for food, [app. shallow, resembling a round tray, for it is said to be] like the xiwaAn ; also called ↓ Taboliy~apN , of which the pl. is TabaAlK . (TA. [See also sad~N , last sentence.]) [And A kind of tray, of wood, used for counting money, &c.; also called ↓ TabolapN : this is app. what is meant by the saying in the S, Tabolu Ald~araAhimi wagayorihaA maEoruwfN ; and by the saying in the O, Tabolapu Ald~aArahimi maEoruwfN .] ― -b3- And A certain sort of garments, or cloths, (Lth, IDrd, O, K, *) upon which is the form of the Tabol [or drum ], (Lth, O, K,) or figured with the like of Tubuwl [or drums ], (T, TA,) of the fabric of El-Yemen, or of Egypt, (K,) or brought from Egypt, and called also ↓ AlT~aboliy~apu and A^arodiyapu AlT~aboli : (Lth, O:) which last appellation is expl. in the A as meaning [ garments of the kind called ] buruwd , worn by the lords, or principal personages, of Egypt. He loves the xaraAj , (O,) or the money of the xaraAj , (K,) without fatigue. (O.) -A2- AlT~abolu signifies also Alxaloqu and Aln~aAsu [i. e. The created beings in general and mankind in particular]: one says, maA A^adoriY A^aY~u AlT~aboli huwa i. e. [ I know not ] what one of mankind he is: (S, O:) and so A^aY~u AlT~aboni huwa . (TA.)

definition: A species of plant, which is eaten;
sourceDefinition: A species of plant, which is eaten; (S, K;) [app. a kind, or species, of fungus; perhaps a species of phallus; ] a plant of the same kind as the *uw^onuwn and the Eurojuwn ; (IAar, T in art. *A^n ;) accord. to Lth, a slender, oblong plant, inclining to redness, and serving as a dibaAg to the stomach [app. meaning a stomachic ], included among medicines, of which there is a bitter sort and a sweet sort; (Msb;) in the M said to be a plant of the sands, long and slender, similar to the fuTor [q. v.], inclining to redness, which dries, and serves as a dibaAg to the stomach; n. un. with p ; on the authority of AHn: it is of two sorts; one sweet, which is the red; and one bitter, which is the white; IAar says that it is a plant of the length of a cubit, having no leaves, as though it were of the same kind as the truffle; (TA;) Az says that the Trvwv of the desert has no leaves (Msb, TA) nor any fruit, (TA,) grows in the sands (Msb, TA) and in the level grounds, (TA,) has in it no acidity, (Msb,) but a sweetness inclining to astringency and bitterness, and is red, with a round head, (Msb, TA,) like the glans of a man's penis: (TA:) [Ibn-Seenà (whom we call Avicenna), in his list of medicinal simples, (book ii., p. 183 of the printed ed.,) describes TaraAviyv as pieces of wood in a rotting state, of the thickness of a finger, and in length less and more, having an astringent taste, and dust-coloured; said to be brought from the desert. See also suwqapN .] The Arabs say, TaraAviyvu laA A^aroTaY lahaA [ Turthoothehs without artáhs ]: because the former grow not save with the latter: a prov., like *aA=niynu laA rimova lahaA : applied to him who is ruined, and has nothing remaining, after having had ancestry and rank and wealth. (TA. [See also art. *A^n , last sentence.]) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) The glans of a man's penis: (K, TA:) so called as being likened to [the head of] the plant above described. (TA.)

definition: A sort of food, called in Pers.
sourceDefinition: A sort of food, called in Pers. laA xi$aho ; (S;) [i. e.] a certain food, like threads, made of flour; (K, TA;) an explanation necessarily implying that it is what is called in Egypt gazolu AlbanaAti : accord. to Sh, a thing made of softened starch; and said by Lth to be a food made by the people of Syria; a word having no n. un.; and what these two say indicates that it is what is called kunaAfap : Lth and Z mention the word as pronounced also with fet-h; but Az says that the pronunciation with fet-h is incorrect. (TA.)

definition: A thing that goes for nothing;
sourceDefinition: A thing that goes for nothing; [as blood that is unretaliated, or uncompensated by a mulct; ] that is of no account, ineffectual, or null; syn. hadarN ; (S, O, K;) [and so ↓ TalofN , as shown by what follows;] as also ↓ TaliyfN . (O, K.) You say, *ahaba damuhu TalafFA , (AA, S, O, K,) and ↓ TalofFA , (AA, O, K,) and ZalafFA and ZalofFA , (AA, O,) His blood went for nothing; as a thing of no account; ineffectually; or in vain; unretaliated, or uncompensated by a mulct; syn. hadarFA , (AA, S, O, K, TA,) and baATilFA : and in like manner, maAluhu [ his property ]. (TA. [See also talafN .]) And Ru-beh says, ↓ kamo mino EidFY A^amowaAluhumo Taliyfu [ How many enemies are there whose possessions are things that have gone for nought ! ]. (O, as an ex. of the last word in the sense of hadar .) ― -b2- And (S, O, K) hence (O) A gift; (S, O, K;) a gift freely bestowed, not for any compensation. (S, TA.) ― -b3- And A thing that is easy; or of light estimation, paltry, or despicable; [as also ZalafN ;] syn. hay~inN . (IF, O, K.) ― -b4- And A redundant portion of a thing: (IF, O, K:) if this be not what is meant by the saying that TalafN is syn. with faDolN , this saying is of no account. (IF, O.)

definition: , (S, L, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, L, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. TumuwHN (K in art. md , and TK) and TimaAHN and TamoHN , (TK,) His sight, or eye, became raised towards it, (S, K,) i. e., a thing: (S:) or became stretched and raised towards it. (L.) And TamaHa bibaSarihi , aor. , (L, Msb,) inf. n. TamoHN , (L,) or TumuwHN , (Msb,) He raised his eyes; (L, Msb;) [and] so baSarahu ↓ A^aTomaHa : (S, K:) or cast his eyes: (L:) towards a thing ( A_ilaY $aYo'K , L, or naHowa $aYo'K , Msb): [said to be] from the phrase jabalN TaAmiHN . (Msb.) And TamaHa baEayonihi , said of a proud man, He raised his eye. (A.) And TamaHato biEayonihaA She (a woman) cast her eye at a man. (L.) And TamaHato [alone], said of a woman, She raised her eyes. (L.) And taTomaHu A_ilaY Alr~ijaAli [ She raises her eyes towards, or looks at, men ]. (S.) ― -b2- And TamaHa , inf. n. TimaAHN and TumuwHN , (A, L, TA,) He (a horse) raised his head and his eyes in his running: (A, TA:) or he raised his fore legs; (L;) and so ↓ Tm~H , inf. n. taTomiyHN : (T, L, K:) [or the former, he was, or became, refractory, and overcame his rider, running away with him: for] TimaAHN is syn. with jimaAHN , (K,) or like jimaAHN : (Yz, S:) one says, farasN fiyhi TimaAHN [ a horse in which is refractoriness, &c.]. (S.) ― -b3- TamaHato , aor. , (L,) inf. n. TimaAHN , (L, K,) is also said of a woman, meaning (assumed tropical:) She was, or became, disobedient to her husband, resisting him, hating him, and deserting him: (L, K: *) and, thus said of a woman, TamaHato , (S, K,) or TamaHato EalaY zawojihaA , (A,) is syn. with, (A, K,) or like, (S,) jamaHato (tropical:) [ she went forth from the place where she used to pass the night, in anger, without the permission of her husband ]: (S, A, K:) and TamaHato mino zawojihaA and jamaHato (tropical:) she went forth from the house, or tent, of her husband, to her own family, before he divorced her. (TA in art. jmE .) And TamaHa , like jamaHa Alyh , said of a man, (assumed tropical:) He hastened, or went quickly, to him, or it, so that his course was not turned for anything. (TA in art. TmH .) ― -b4- TamaHa , inf. n. TimaAHN , also signifies (assumed tropical:) He was proud, and boastful; because he who is so exalts himself. (L.) ― -b5- And TamaHa fiY Als~awomi (assumed tropical:) He went far beyond what was right, or just, in making a bargain for his merchandise. (Lh, L.) And TamaHa , (S,) or TamaHa fiY AlT~alabi , (K,) (assumed tropical:) He went far in search; (S, K;) so accord. to some. (S.) [ TamaHa A_ilaY kul~i $aYo' , said of the heart, app. means (assumed tropical:) It aspired to everything: see its part. n., TaAmiHN .] ― -b6- TamaHa Al$~uxobu (assumed tropical:) The extended stream of milk from the udder fell upon the ground so as to be unprofitable. (Provs. of Meyd, section $ : see $uxobN .) ― -b7- TamaHa bihi (assumed tropical:) He made, or caused, him, or it, to go, go away, or pass away; took away, carried off, or went away with, him, or it. (K.) ― -b8- And TamaHotu Al$~aYo'a [if not a mistranscription for Tam~aHotu biAl$~aYo'i ] (tropical:) I cast the thing in the air. (A.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. TanFY , (S,) said of a camel, He had his spleen adhering to his side in consequence of vehement thirst: (S:) or, said of a man, he had his spleen and his lungs adhering to the ribs on the left side, (K, TA,) so that, sometimes, they become putrid and black; but mostly this is the case in camels; (TA;) as also ↓ ATnY : (K:) or he (a man) had a tertian fever, and his spleen in consequence became enlarged: (Lh, * TA:) and, said of a camel, his spleen became enlarged in consequence of the [ disease of the lungs called ] nuHaAz . (Lh, TA.) [And Taniy^a is a dial. var. thereof.] ― -b2- And, said of a man, i. q. DaniYa [i. e. He was, or became, slender, and small in body: or diseased, disordered, or sick: or lean, or emaciated: &c.]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. taToniyapN , He treated him to cure him of the disorder of the spleen mentioned above; (S, K;) namely, a camel, (S,) or a man: (K:) and he cauterized him (i. e. his camel) in his side; (K, TA;) or, as in the Nawádir of Lh, Tn~Y baEiyrahu fiY janobayohi he cauterized his camel [ in his sides ] by reason of the disorder above mentioned: and the cure [or curing] of that disorder is [also] the taking a wooden peg, and laying him [i. e. the camel] upon his side on the ground, and making, between his ribs, incisions [ therewith ], not penetrating through. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: The inf. n. TawaAfN primarily signifies, accord. to Er-Rághib, The act of going, or walking, in an absolute sense: or the going, or walking, around, or otherwise. (MF, TA.) TawofN (S, O, Msb, K) and TawaAfN (O, Msb, K, and mentioned also in the S but not there said to be an inf. n.) and TawafaAnN , (S, O, K,) [and perhaps TuwfaAnN , q. v.,] He went round or round about, circuited, or circuited around, or compassed, (Msb, TA,) the thing, (S, Msb,) or the Kaabeh; (O, K;) and so TaAfa , aor. yaTiyfu ; (Msb; [but this I think doubtful;]) and ↓ tTw~f , (S, Msb, K,) and ↓ AiT~aw~afa , a variation of that next preceding, (Msb, TA,) inf. n. AiT~iw~aAfN ; (TA;) and ↓ AstTAf , (S, Msb, K,) as also ↓ AstTAfhu ; (TA;) and bihi ↓ ATAf , (Msb,) or Ealayohi ; (TA;) and ↓ Tw~f , inf. n. ↓ taTowiyfN ; (K;) or this last signifies he did so much, or often. TawofN and TawafaAnN and maTaAfN , He went round about [or round about among ] the people, or party; as also ↓ ATAf : the aor. of the former verb occurs in the Kur lvi. 17 and lxxvi. 19, trans. by means of EalaY . (S, O, K.)

definition: An overpowering rain: and overpowering water, [a meaning erroneously assigned in the CK to Taw~aAf instead of TuwfaAn ,] that covers [or overwhelms ] everything;
sourceDefinition: An overpowering rain: and overpowering water, [a meaning erroneously assigned in the CK to Taw~aAf instead of TuwfaAn ,] that covers [or overwhelms ] everything; (S, K, TA;) in the common conventional acceptation, water abounding to the utmost degree; [i. e. a flood, or deluge; ] such as befell the people of Noah; (TA;) or TuwfaAnu AlmaA='i signifies the water that covers [or overwhelms ] everything: (Msb:) and a drowning torrent: (K:) and (assumed tropical:) much of anything, [like as we say a flood of anything,] such as includes the generality of persons, or things, within its compass: (K, TA:) and particularly (assumed tropical:) death; or quick, or quick and wide-spreading, death; or death commonly, or generally, prevailing; (TA;) or quick, or quick and wide-spreading, death, commonly, or generally, prevailing: and (assumed tropical:) quick [ and extensive ] slaughter: (K:) and (assumed tropical:) any accident [or evil accident ] that besets a man: and (assumed tropical:) trial, or affliction: (TA:) and El-'Ajjáj likens to the rain, or water, thus called, the darkness of night; using the phrase TuwfaAnu AlZ~alaAmi ; (Kh, S;) by which he means (assumed tropical:) the intensity of the darkness of the night: (TA:) TuwfaAnN is said to be a pl. [or coll. gen. n.]; (Msb, TA;) and its sing. [or n. un.] is TuwfaAnapN , (S, Msb, K, TA,) accord. to analogy: (S:) thus says Akh: (S, TA:) or it is an inf. n., like rujoHaAnN and nuqoSaAnN ; and is from TaAfa , aor. yaTuwfu : (Msb, TA:) thus says Abu-l- 'Abbás; and he says that there is no need of seeking for it a sing.: some say that it is of the measure fuloEaAnN , from TafaA AlmaA='u , aor. yaTofuw , meaning “ the water rose, ” or “ became high; ” the l being transposed to the place of the E ; but this is strange. (TA.)

definition: A detached, or distinct, part or portion;
sourceDefinition: A detached, or distinct, part or portion; a piece, or bit; [or somewhat; ] of a thing: (S, Msb, K:) and a firoqap of men [i. e. a party, portion, division, or class, thereof; as those of one profession or trade: a body, or distinct community: a sect: a corps: and sometimes a people, or nation ]: (Msb:) and a company, or congregated body, (Msb, KL,) of men, at least consisting of three; and sometimes applied to one; and two: (Msb:) or one: and more than one: (S, K:) so, accord. to I' Ab, in the Kur xxiv. 2: (S:) or up to a thousand: (Mujáhid, K:) or at least two men: ('Atà, K:) or one man; (K;) as is said also on the authority of Mujáhid; (TA;) so that it is syn. with nafosN [as meaning a single person, or an individual ]: (K:) [and sometimes it is applied to a distinct number, or herd &c., of animals:] Er-Rághib says that when a plural or collective number is meant thereby, it is [what lexicologists term] a pl. of TaAy^ifN ; and when one is meant thereby, it may be a pl. metonymically used as a sing., or it may be considered as of the class of raAwiyapN and Eal~aAmapN and the like: (TA:) [pl. TawaAy^ifu .] ― -b2- See also TaAy^ifN , last sentence but one.

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. Zan~N , (Msb,) [ He thought, opined, supposed, or conjectured: and he doubted: and he knew, but not by ocular perception: see Zan~N below:] you say, Zananotu Al$~aYo'a , aor. A^aZun~uhu , inf. n. Zan~N ; and ↓ AiZ~ananotuhu and AiZoTananotuhu ; and ↓ taZan~anotuhu and taZan~ayotuhu , this last formed by changing the last n into Y : [i. e. I thought the thing, &c:] and Lh mentions, as heard from the Benoo-Suleym, Zanotu *aAka i. e. Zananotu *Ak [ I thought that, &c.] like Zalotu and other instances of the dial. of Suleym. (M.) [In the first of the senses expl. above, it governs two objective complements, which are originally an inchoative and an enunciative:] you say, Zananotuka zayodFA [ I thought thee Zeyd, originally I thought thou wast Zeyd ], and Zananotu zayodFA A_iy~aAka [ I thought Zeyd thee, originally I thought Zeyd was thou ], denoting by a pronoun what is originally an inchoative [in the former phrase] and what is originally an enunciative [in the latter phrase]. (S, TA.) It is also used [in this sense] in the same manner as a verb signifying an oath, the Arabs giving it the same kind of complement, saying, Zananotu laEabodu A@ll~`hi xayorN minoka [ I thought surely 'Abd-Allah was better than thou ]. (S in art. drd .) [ Zan~a bihi ka*aA means I thought of him, or it, such a thing: and I thought such a thing to be in him, or it: and is used in relation to good and to evil.] It is said in the Kur [xxxiii. 10], wataTun~uwna biA@ll~`hi A@lZ~unuwnaA [ And ye were thinking, of God, various thoughts ]. (M.) Accord. to Sb, Zananotu bihi means I made him, or it, the place [i. e. object ] of my Zan~ [or thought, &c.]. (M.) [In all these exs. the verb denotes a state of mind between doubt and certainty, but the latter is predominant: and hence Zan~a sometimes means He doubted: and sometimes, he knew, by considering with endeavour to understand, not by ocular perception; being more frequently used in this sense than as meaning “ he doubted, ” though not so frequently as it is in the sense of “ he thought, ” whence the meaning “ he knew ” is held by some to be tropical.] A_in~aY , Zananotu A^an~iY mulaAqK HisaAbiyaho , in the Kur [lxix. 20], means Verily I knew [ that I should meet with my reckoning ]. (T.) And A@l~a*iyna yaZun~uwna A^an~ahumo mulaAquw rab~ihimo , in the same [ii. 43], means Who know [ that they shall meet their Lord, lit., be meeters of their Lord ]. (Msb.) And Zananotu maA qaAla , occurring in a trad., means I knew [ what he meant to say by his making a sign with his hand]. (TA.) ― -b2- Zananotuhu , (M, Mgh, Msb,) aor. as above, (Msb,) and so the inf. n., (M,) signifies also I suspected him; thought evil of him; (M, Mgh, Msb;) and (M) so ↓ AiZ~ananotuhu (S, M, Mgh, K) and AiZoTananotuhu (M, TA) and AiT~ananotuhu . (TA.) [Thus, too, ↓ A^aZonanotuhu accord. to several copies of the S and accord. to the CK; but this is app. a mistranscription.] In the saying of Ibn-Seereen, lamo fiY qatoli EuvomaAna ↓ yakuno EaliY~N yuZ~an~u , (T, S, K, but in the T maA kaAn ,) meaning Alee was not suspected [ in the case of the slaying of 'Othmán ], (T,) yuZ~an~u is of the measure yufotaEalu , originally yuZotan~u : (T, S, K:) so says A'Obeyd: (T:) or, as some relate it, the word is yuT~an~u . (TA.) One says, bika*aA ↓ huwa yuZ~an~u and yuT~an~u , meaning He is suspected of such a thing. (TA in art. Tn .) And Tananotu bizayodK and Zananotu zayodFA I suspected Zeyd: in this sense the verb has a single objective complement. (TA.)

definition: is a simple subst.
sourceDefinition: is a simple subst. as well as an inf. n.; (TA;) and signifies Thought, opinion, supposition, or conjecture: (Er-Rághib, Mgh, TA:) or a preponderant belief, with the admission that the contrary may be the case: (KT, El-Munáwee, TA:) or a preponderating wavering between the two extremes in indecisive belief: (K:) or an inference from a sign, or mark, or token; when strong, leading to knowledge; and when weak, not exceeding the limit of wahom : (Er-Rághib, TA:) or doubt or uncertainty; (T, M;) or it has this meaning also; (Er-Rághib, TA;) contr. of yaqiynN : (Msb:) and sometimes it is put in the place, (S, K,) or used in the sense, (Mgh, Msb,) of EilomN , (S, Mgh, K,) or yaqiynN , (Msb,) [i. e. knowledge, or certainty, ] in which sense it is [held by some to be] tropical; (Mgh;) or it signifies also knowledge, or certainty, ( yaqiynN , T, M,) such as is obtained by considering with endeavour to understand, not by ocular perception, (M,) or not such as relates to an object of sense: (MF:) and it also means suspicion, or evil opinion: (Er-Rághib, TA: [but in this last sense, Zin~apN is more common:]) as a subst., (TA,) its pl. is ZunuwnN and A^aZaAniynu , (M, K, TA,) the latter anomalous, or (as ISd says, TA) it may be pl. of ↓ A^uZonuwnapN , but this I do not know. (M, TA.) One says, huwa say~iy^u AlZ~an~i bikul~i A^aHadK [ He is evil in opinion of everyone ]. (M.) [And saA='a Zan~uhu bifulaAnK His opinion of such a one was evil. ] And Eilomuhu biAl$~aYo'i ZunuwnN [ His knowledge is but opinions ]; meaning that no confidence is to be placed in him. (TA.)

definition: A man who thinks evil (S, M) of everyone.
sourceDefinition: A man who thinks evil (S, M) of everyone. (M.) ― -b2- A man possessing little good or goodness: or, as some say, of whom one asks [ a thing ] thinking that he will refuse, and who is as he was thought to be: (M:) [or] ↓ ZaniynN has this latter meaning. (TA.) ― -b3- A man in whose goodness no trust, or confidence, is to be placed. (M.) And Anything in which no trust, or confidence, is to be placed, (M, TA,) of water, and of other things; (TA;) as also ↓ ZaniynN . (M, TA.) A well ( biy^orN ) having little water, (S, M, K,) in the water of which no trust, or confidence, is to be placed: (M:) or a well, (S, K,) or a drinkingplace, (M,) of which one knows not whether there be in it water or not: (S, M, K:) or water which one imagines, or supposes, to exist, but of which one is not sure. (TA.) kul~u maniy~apK ZanuwnN A_il~aA Alqatola fiY sabiyli A@ll~`hi is a saying mentioned, but not expl., by IAar; [app. meaning Every death is doubtful as to its consequence except slaughter in the way, or cause, of God; but ISd says,] in my opinion the meaning is that it is of little good and profit. (M.) dayonN ZanuwnN means A debt of which one knows not whether he who owes it will pay it or not: (A'Obeyd, T, S, M, * K:) it is said in a trad. of 'Omar that there is no poorrate in the case of such a debt. (TA.) ― -b4- Also A man suspected in relation to his intellect, or intelligence. (Aboo-Tálib, TA.) And A woman suspected in relation to her grounds of pretension to respect, or honour, on account of lineage &c. (TA.) And A woman of noble rank or quality, who is taken in marriage, (M, K,) from a desire of obtaining off spring by her, when she is advanced in age. (M.) ― -b5- Also A weak man. (K. [See also ZanynN .]) ― -b6- And A man having little artifice, cunning, ingenuity, or skill. (K.)

definition: , (M, Mgh, Msb, TA,) of which maZan~apN , mentioned by Ibn-Málik and others, and miZan~apN , are dial.
sourceDefinition: , (M, Mgh, Msb, TA,) of which maZan~apN , mentioned by Ibn-Málik and others, and miZan~apN , are dial. vars., (TA,) or [rather] maZin~apu $aYo'K , (IF, S, Msb, K, TA,) signifies The place, (IF, S, Msb, K, TA,) and the accustomed place, (IF, S, Msb, TA,) in which is thought to be the existence, (S, K, TA,) of a thing; (IF, S, Msb, K, TA;) [ a place ] where a thing is thought to be: (M:) or it signifies, (Mgh, Msb,) or signifies also, (S,) a place where a thing is known to be: (S, Mgh, Msb:) [ a thing, and a person, in which, or in whom, a thing, or quality, is thought, supposed, presumed, suspected, inferred, known, or accustomed, to be, or exist: ] accord. to IAth, by rule it should be maZan~apN : (TA:) [it may therefore be properly rendered a cause of thinking, &c., the existence of a thing; and maZin~apN lika*aA may be well expl. as meaning a thing, and a person, that occasions one's thinking, supposing, presuming suspecting, inferring, or knowing, the existence of such a thing or quality, in it, or in him: and hence, an indication, or evidence, or a symptom, diagnostic, characteristic, sign, mark, or token, of the existence of such a thing or quality: ] the pl. is maZaAn~u . (M, Mgh, Msb, TA.) One says, mawoDiEu ka*aA maZin~apN mino fulaAnK i. e. Such a place is a place in which such a one is known [&c.] to be. (S, TA.) And fulaAnN maZin~apN mino ka*aA i. e. Such a one is one in whom such a thing, or quality, is known [&c.] to be. (Lh, T.) And fulaAnN maZin~apN liloxayori i. e. Such a one is one in whom good, or goodness, is thought [&c.] to be. (Ham p. 437.) And En-Nábighah says, faA_ino yaku EaAmirN qado qaAla jaholFA faA_in~a maZin~apa Aljaholi Al$~abaAbu [ And if 'Ámir has spoken ignorantly, verily youthfulness is a state in which ignorance is usually found to exist ]: (S, Msb: *) or, as some relate the verse, Als~ibaAbu [so that the meaning is, mutual reviling is an act in which &c.]: (S:) or, accord. to another relation, the latter hemistich is faA_in~a maTiy~apa Aljaholi Al$~abaAbu (S, * TA;) because one finds it [i. e. youthfulness] to be easy like as he does the beast on which one rides. (TA.) And one says also, Talabahu maZaAn~ahu [ He sought him, or it, in the places where he, or it, was thought to be; ] meaning, by night and by day. (TA.) And A_in~ahu lamaZin~apN A^ano yafoEala *`lika i. e. Verily he is apt, meet, fitted, or suited, for one to think of his doing that: and in like manner one says of two, and of a pl. number, and of a female. (Lh, M.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, Msb,) inf. n. EajomN (S, Msb, K) and EujuwmN , (K,) He bit it: (Msb, K:) and he chewed it: (Msb:) or he chewed it for the purpose of eating or of trial: (K:) or he bit it with the lateral teeth, not with the central incisors: (TA:) or he bit it, namely, a piece of wood, or a stick, or rod, or the like, in order to know whether it were hard or fragile: (S:) or he tried it with his lateral teeth in order that he might know, or prove, its hardness: and he bit it, namely, a gaming-arrow known for winning, between two lateral teeth, in order to make upon it a mark by which he might know it. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (TA,) (tropical:) He tried, tested, or proved, him. (K, TA.) And Eajamotu Euwdahu (assumed tropical:) I tried, tested, or proved his case, and knew his state, or condition. (S, TA.) And Eajamatohu AlA^umuwru (assumed tropical:) Affairs exercised him so as to render him strong for them, and habituated, or inured, to them. (TA.) And Kabeesah Ibn-Jábir says, AlA^umuwra waEaAjamatoniY ↓ waEaAjamotu kaA^an~iY kunotu fiY AlA^umami AlxawaAliY [(assumed tropical:) And I have tried affairs, and they have tried me, as though I were of the generations that have passed away ]; meaning, as though I were one of the long-lived, by reason of my many trials. (Ham p. 340.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] one says, Alv~uworu yaEojumu qaronahu (assumed tropical:) The bull smites the tree with his horn to try, or test, it. (S, K.) ― -b4- And Eajama Als~ayofa , (S, K,) inf. n. EajomN , (TA,) (assumed tropical:) He shook the sword to try, or test, it. (S, K.) ― -b5- maA Eajamatoka EayoniY muno*u ka*aA means (assumed tropical:) My eye has not seen thee since such a time; (S, K, TA;) and is said by a man to one with whom his [last] meeting was long past. (TA.) An Arab of the desert is related to have said, taEojumuka EayoniY , meaning (assumed tropical:) [ My eye seems to know thee; or] it seems to me that I have seen thee. (TA.) And one says, raA^ayotu fulaAnFA fajaEalato EayoniY taEojumuhu i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ I saw such a one, ] and my eye seemed to know him, (Lh, S, K, TA,) not knowing him perfectly, as though not certain of him. (TA.) And EajamuwniY (assumed tropical:) They knew me. (TA.) ― -b6- And [hence, app.,] one says, naZarotu fiY AlkitaAbi faEajamotu , meaning (assumed tropical:) [ I looked into the book, or writing, and ] I did not know surely its letters. (TA.) ― -b7- See also 4. -A2- Eajuma , [aor. ,] inf. n. EujomapN , He had an impotence, or an impediment, or a difficulty, in his speech, or utterance; and [ a barbarousness, or vitiousness, therein, especially in speaking Arabic; (see EujomapN below;) i. e.] a want of clearness, perspicuousness, distinctness, chasteness, or correctness, therein. (Msb.)

definition: He made it (i. e. speech, or language, S, K, or a thing, TA) to want, or be without, or to have a quality the contrary of, clearness, perspicuousness, or distinctness; (S, Msb, K, * TA;) or [ to be...
sourceDefinition: He made it (i. e. speech, or language, S, K, or a thing, TA) to want, or be without, or to have a quality the contrary of, clearness, perspicuousness, or distinctness; (S, Msb, K, * TA;) or [ to be barbarous, or vitious, i. e.] to want, or be without, chasteness, or correctness. (K, * TA.) Ru-beh says, [in some verses very differently cited in different copies of the S,] of him who attempts poetry without having knowledge thereof, yuriydu A^ano yuEoribahu fayuEojimuho [ He desires to make it clear, &c., and he makes it to want clearness, &c.]. (S.) ― -b2- And He dotted it, or pointed it, (S, K,) namely, a letter, (S,) or a writing; (K;) he removed its Eujomap [or want of clearness, &c.,] by means of dots, or [ diacritical ] points, (Nh, Msb, TA,) and [ the signs called ] $akol , [but see $kl ,] which distinguished it, namely, a letter, from other letters; the A denoting privation; (Msb;) as ISd holds to be the case; (TA;) and so ↓ Ej~mhu , (S, * K,) inf. n. taEojiymN ; (S;) and ↓ Eajamahu , (K,) inf. n. EajomN ; (S;) for J's assertion [in the S] that one should not say Eajamotu is a mistake: (K:) this last verb, however, which J thus disallows, is disallowed also by Th, in his Fs, and by most of the expositors thereof; and J confined himself to the correct and chaste. (TA.) ― -b3- And He locked it; namely, a door. definition: He was unable to speak: (TA:) he was silent, mute, or speechless;
sourceDefinition: He was unable to speak: (TA:) he was silent, mute, or speechless; (K, TA;) said of a man. (TA.) And AisotaEojamati Ald~aAru Eano jawaAbi saAy^ilihaA [ The dwelling kept silence from replying to its interrogator ]: and Imra-el-Keys says, Sam~a SadaAhaA waEafaA rasomuhaA waA@sotaEojamato Eano manoTiqi Als~aAy^ili [ Its echo has become dumb, and its trace has become effaced, and it has become in the state of keeping silence from answering the speech of the interrogator ]: he makes AstEjmt trans. by means of En because it is used in the sense of sakatato . (TA.) ― -b2- One says also, AstEjm Ealayohi AlkalaAmu , (S,) or EalayonaA , (Msb,) meaning Speech was as though it were closed against him, or us; or he, or we, became impeded in speech, unable to speak, or tongue-tied; syn. Aisotabohama : (S, Msb:) and Elyh AlklAm ↓ AnEjm ; [which means the same;] syn. AinoTabaqa and Ainogalaqa . (K * and TA in art. Tbq .) And accord. to the K, one says, AstEjm AlqiraA='apa , meaning He was unable to perform [or continue ] the recitation, or reading, by reason of the overcoming of drowsiness: but what is said in the Nh and other works is AisotaEoHamato Ealayohi qiraA='atuhu i. e. His recitation, or reading, was cut short, and he was unable to perform [or continue ] it, by reason of drowsiness: and it is also expl. as meaning he was, or became, impeded in his recitation, or reading, and unable to perform [or continue ] it, as though he became one in whom was Eujomap . (TA.) ― -b3- And AstEjm Alxabaru means The information, or narration, was dubious, confused, vague, or difficult to be understood or expressed; or was not to be understood or expressed; as though it were closed [ against the hearer or speaker ]; syn. Aisotabohama , and Aisotagolaqa . (Msb in art. bhm .)

definition: [ Foreigners, as meaning ] others than Arabs;
sourceDefinition: [ Foreigners, as meaning ] others than Arabs; such as are not Arabs; [often used as implying disparagement, like barbarians; and often especially meaning Persians; ] (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) as also ↓ EujomN , [of which see an ex. in a verse of Lebeed cited voce raAziqiY~N ,] (S, Msb, K,) or this latter may be a pl. of the former: (TA:) ↓ EajamiY~N (of which A^aEojaAmN is pl., TA) signifies one thereof; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) one who is of the race of the Eajam ; (K;) though he may be chaste, or correct, in [ the Arabic ] speech; (Mgh, K;) the Y denoting unity; but it is also the relative Y , and thus one may apply to an Arab the appellation ↓ EajamiY~N as meaning called thus in relation to the Eajam : (Msb:) and one says also ↓ rajulN A^aEojamu [ a man not of the Arabs ]: and ↓ qawomN A^aEojamu [ a people, or party, not of the Arabs ]. (K.) -A2- Also The stones of dates (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and of the drupes of the lote-tree (Msb) and of grapes (Mgh, Msb) and of raisins and of pomegranates and the like, (Mgh,) or also of other things, (Msb,) or the similar stones of anything, (K,) or also whatever is in the interior of a thing that is eaten such as the raisin and the like; (S;) and ↓ EujaAmN signifies the same: (K:) the vulgar say ↓ Eajom : (Yaakoob, S:) [see also giyDN , in an explanation of which EajamN is evidently, I think, used as meaning the heart (commonly termed jum~aAr q. v.) of the palm-tree: ] the n. un. is EajamapN , (S, Mgh, Msb,) which is incorrectly expl. by AHn as meaning a grape-stone when it germinates. (ISd, TA.) -A3- Also Camels that bite, or chew, the [ trees called ] EiDaAh and the tragacanths and [ other ] thorny trees, and satisfy themselves therewith so as to be in no need of the [ plants called ] HamoD . (S.)

definition: One having an impotence, or an impediment, or a difficulty, in speech, or utterance, (S, Msb,) though he may be clear, perspicuous, distinct, chaste, or correct, in speaking a foreign language;
sourceDefinition: One having an impotence, or an impediment, or a difficulty, in speech, or utterance, (S, Msb,) though he may be clear, perspicuous, distinct, chaste, or correct, in speaking a foreign language; (S;) and [ barbarous, or vitious therein; i. e.] not clear, perspicuous, distinct, chaste, or correct, therein; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) meaning, in speaking Arabic, (S, Mgh, Msb, * K, *) though he may be an Arab; (S, Mgh, Msb;) and ↓ A^aEojamiY~N signifies the same, (Mgh, Msb, K,) and therefore, if applied to an Arab, it does not imply reproach; (Msb; [but it is said in the Mgh that this demands consideration;]) or this latter epithet is applied to a tongue, or speech, and to a book, or writing, but not to a man unless it be syn. with the former epithet: (S:) the fem. of the former is EajomaA='u : (S, Mgh, Msb:) and the dual masc. A^aEojamaAni (S) and fem. EajomaAwaAni ; (Har p. 226;) and the pl. masc. A^aEojamuwna (S, Msb, TA) and A^aEaAjimu (S, TA) and EujomaAnN : (TA:) and the pl. of ↓ A^aEojamiY~N is A^aEojamiy~uwna . (Msb.) See also EajamN , first sentence, in two places. ― -b2- Also Dumb; speechless; destitute of the faculty of speech; (K, TA:) unable to speak; and so ↓ musotaEojimN : (S, TA:) fem. of the former as above. (TA.) ― -b3- Hence, (S,) by predominance of its application, (Mgh,) EajomaA='u signifies A beast, or brute; syn. bahiymapN ; (S, Mgh, K;) and so ↓ musotaEojimN [or the fem. of this]: (TA:) pl. of the former in this sense, as a subst., EajomaAwaAtN : (Har p. 13:) [and] EajomaA='u is applied [also] as an epithet to a beast, or brute, ( bhymp ,) for the like reason. (Msb.) It is said in a trad., juroHu AlEajomaA='i jubaArN [expl. in art. jbr ]. (S, Mgh.) ― -b4- [Hence also] faHolN A^aEojamu signifies A stallion [ camel ] that brays in a $iqo$iqap [or faucial bag ] to which there is no perforation, so that the sound does not issue from it: and they approve of the sending such among the $awol [or she-camels that have passed seven or eight months since the period of their bringing forth] because he usually begets females. (TA.) ― -b5- (tropical:) The prayer of the daytime is termed EajomaA='u because the reciting [of the Kur-án] therein is inaudible; (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA;) i. e. the prayer of noon and of afternoon; (TA;) and these two together are termed AlEajomaAwaAni . (Har p. 226.) ― -b6- mawojN A^aEojamu means (tropical:) Waves that do not sprinkle their water, and of which no sound is heard. (S, K.) ― -b7- And EajomaA='u [or ramolapN EajomaA='u ?] (assumed tropical:) A tract of sand in which are no trees. (IAar, K.)

(TA.)

sourceDefinition: [pass. part. n. of 4: and also an inf. n. of that verb]. Huruwfu AlmuEojami , an appellation of The letters of the alphabet ( AlHuruwf AlmuqaT~aEap ) [ of the language of the Arabs ], most of which are distinguished by being dotted from the letters of other peoples, means Huruwfu AlxaT~i AlmuEojami [ the letters of the dotted character ]: (S:) or by AlmuEojami is meant AlA_iEojaAmi , it being an inf. n., like Almudoxal (S, K) and Almuxoraj , (S,) so that the meaning of Huruwfu AlmuEojami is [ the letters ] of which a property is the being dotted: (S, K:) of which explanations, the latter is held by Mbr and IB and others to be the more correct. (L, TA.) ― -b2- Also, applied to a door, Locked. (S, K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. (S, O, Msb) and , (S, O,) inf. n. EuzuwbN , (S, Msb,) He, (a man, S, O,) or it, (a thing, Msb,) was, or became, distant, or remote; (S, O, Msb;) and absent; Ean~iY from me: (S, O:) or ↓ AEzb has the former meaning: (K:) and Eazaba , aor. and , (Msb, K,) inf. n. as above, (K,) signifies he, or it, was, or became, absent, (Msb, K,) and concealed: (Msb:) and went away, or departed. (K, TA.) You say, Eazaba bihaA , referring to sheep or goats, He went to a distance, or far off, with them: so in a trad.: or, as some relate it, bhA ↓ Ez~b , meaning he went with them to a remote pasturage: and he pastured them (namely, camels,) at a distance from the place of abode of the tribe, not repairing, or returning, to them [ in the evening ]: and ↓ tEz~b , and thus the verb is written in copies of the K in a place where some copies have yaEozubu , occurs in the phrase tEz~b Eano A^aholihi wamaAlihi [ He went away to a distance from his family and his cattle, or camels &c.]. (TA.) And Eazabati AlA_ibilu The camels went away to a distance in the pasturage, not returning in the evening: (S, O:) and in like manner one says of sheep or goats. (O.) And laA yaEozubu Eano Eilomihi $aYo'N Nothing is absent from his (God's) knowledge. (TA. [See Kur x.62 and xxxiv. 3.]) And Eazaba Tuhoru AlmuroA^api [ The woman's state of pureness from the menstrual discharge was a remote thing ] means (assumed tropical:) the woman's husband was absent from her: (K:) or [rather] is said of the woman when her husband is absent from her. (S, O.) And Eazaba Eano fulaAnK Hilomuhu [ Such a one's forbearance quitted him ]; (S, O;) as also ↓ AEzb . (O.) ― -b2- Also, aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. EuzobapN and EuzuwbapN , (Msb, MF, TA,) or these are simple substs., (S, K,) (assumed tropical:) He was without a wife; or in a state of celibacy. (Msb, K.) [And app. Eazabato is said in like manner of a woman, meaning (assumed tropical:) She was without a husband. See also 5.] ― -b3- And Eazabati AlA^aroDu (assumed tropical:) The land, whether fruitful or unfruitful, was, or became, destitute of inhabitants; had in it no one. (S, O, K.)

definition: [correctly thus, but in the sense here following written in the TA without any syll.
sourceDefinition: [correctly thus, but in the sense here following written in the TA without any syll. signs, and in the O written Eiz~abN ,] A man who goes away to a distance into the country, or in the land. (O, TA.) [And One who goes far away with his camels to pasture: pl. A^aEozaAbN . (See also EaziybN and EaAzibN and muEozibN and miEozaAbapN .)] hiraAwapu AlA^aEozaAbi means The staff of those who go far away with their camels to pasture; and a horse is likened thereto, (S, O, TA,) on account of its compactness and smoothness; so in a marginal note in the L: (TA:) [Sgh, however, says,] thus in some of the lexicons, but in my opinion, (O,) it was the name of a mare which was not to be outstripped, and which was thus called because her owner gave her gratuitously for the use of those of his people who had no wives, who made predatory attacks upon her, and when one of them acquired for himself property and a wife, he resigned her to another of his people: (O, K: *) whence the prov. A^aEaz~u mino hiraAwapi AlA^aEozaAbi [ More highly esteemed than Hiráwet-el-Aazáb ]. (O.) See an ex. in a verse cited voce EadiydN . ― -b2- See also EaAzibN . ― -b3- Also Whatever is alone, solitary, or apart from others. (TA.) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) A man having no wife; (Ks, S, Mgh, O, Msb, K;) as also ↓ EaAzibN , (Msb, * TA,) which is the original; (Msb;) and ↓ EaziybN , and ↓ miEozaAbapN [which see below]; (K;) but not ↓ A^aEozaAbu , (Mgh, O, Msb, K,) this being disallowed by AHát, (O, Msb,) and others; (TA;) or it is rare; (K;) but it occurs in a trad.; (Mgh, O;) and some allow it: (O, Msb:) the pl. of the first is A^aEozaAbN , (O, K,) or Euz~aAbN , (S, * Msb,) which is thus because the original form of the sing. is considered as being ↓ EaAzibN , this pl. being like kuf~aArN as pl. of kaAfirN , (Msb,) or EazabN has both of these pls., (O,) or Euz~aAbN is pl. of ↓ EaAzibN , (TA,) and is applied to men and to (assumed tropical:) women as meaning having no spouses: (S, TA:) EazabapN is applied to (assumed tropical:) a woman [as meaning having no husband ], (Ks, S, O, Msb, K,) and (O, Msb, K) so EazabN ; (Zj, Kz, Mgh, O, Msb, K;) and if A^aEozabu be applied to a man, ↓ EazobaA='u , may by rule be applied to a woman; and the pl. of EazabapN is EazabaAtN : (Msb:) or, accord. to Zj, EazabapN is a mistake of Abu-l-'Abbás [i. e. Th], and EazabN is used as an epithet of a man and of a woman, like as is xaSomN , and does not assume a dual form nor a pl. nor a fem. form, because it is originally an inf. n.; MF, however, denies that we have any authority for calling EazabN an inf. n.: he considers it to be a simple epithet, like HasanN &c.; and if used in the fem. sense without the termination p otherwise than by poetic license, to be an anomalous epithet, like EaAnisN , which is applied alike to a man and to a woman: the phrase rajulaAni EazabaAni is also mentioned: and the saying A_in~ahu laEazabN lazabN [in which the latter epithet is merely an imitative sequent corrobative of the former], and A_in~ahaA laEazabapN lazabapN : and EazabN is said to be [also] a quasi-pl. n. [of EaAzibN ], like as xadamN is of xaAdimN . (TA.)

definition: Distant, or remote: (Msb, TA:) applied in this sense to herbage: (S, K:) or, applied to herbage, such as has not been depastured at all, nor trodden: and, accord.
sourceDefinition: Distant, or remote: (Msb, TA:) applied in this sense to herbage: (S, K:) or, applied to herbage, such as has not been depastured at all, nor trodden: and, accord. to the A, only such as is in a desert in which is no seed-produce: (TA:) and it is likewise applied to meadows ( rawoDN ) [app. as meaning distant, or remote ]; as also ↓ EaziybN . (A, TA.) In the following saying, waSadorK A^araAHa All~ayolu EaAziba ham~ihi taDaAEafa fiyhi AlHuzonu mino kul~i jaAnibi (tropical:) [ In many a bosom whose remote (or long-past ) anxiety night has brought back, grief has multiplied from every quarter ], it is used metaphorically. (A.) And [in like manner,] in a trad. of 'Átikeh, qahun~a hawaA='N waAlHuluwmu EawaAzibu means (assumed tropical:) And they are devoid of reason, the intel-lects [being] far away: EawaAzibu here being pl. of EaAzibN . (L, TA.) And [in a similar manner,] EawaAzibu AlA^aTohaAri [in which EawaAzibu is pl. of EaAzibapN ] is applied as an epithet to women whose husbands are absent: (S and O and TA, from a verse of En-Ná- bighah Edh-Dhubyánee: [for the lit. meaning, see 1, latter half:]) ― -b2- [for] EaAzibN signifies also Absent; and concealed. (Msb.) ― -b3- It is also applied to sheep or goats, ( $aA='N , O, TA, and ganamN , O,) and to camels, ( A_ibilN , O,) meaning Remote in the pasturage, (O, TA,) that do not return in the evening, (O,) or that do not repair to the place of alighting and abode [ of their owners ] in the night: (TA:) and [in like manner] ↓ EazabN is applied to cattle, or camels &c., ( maAlN , A, O, TA,) meaning that go away to a distance from their owners. (O.) See also EaziybN [which, thus applied, is a quasi-pl. n. of EaAzibN ]. And EaAzibapN is likewise applied to camels (O, K) as meaning That go far away to pasture: (O, K: *) so in the prov. A_in~amaA A@$otarayotu Alganama Hi*aAra AlEaAzibapi [ I only bought the sheep, or goats, in fear of loosing those that go far away to pasture ]: said by a man who had camels, and sold them, and bought sheep, or goats, lest they [the camels] should go far away to pasture; and his sheep, or goats, did so: (O, K:) it is applied to the case of him who acts with gentleness [or precaution] in the easiest of affairs, and has unexpected difficulty, or trouble, inseparable from him. (O.) ― -b4- See also EazabN , in three places. ― -b5- And see muEaz~ibapN .

definition: A man who goes away to a distance with his cattle, or camels &c.
sourceDefinition: A man who goes away to a distance with his cattle, or camels &c., (S, A, O, K,) from others, in the pasturage; (S, O;) as also ↓ miEozaAbN : (A, O, K:) accord. to Az, the former is the only epithet of the measure mifoEaAlapN , except mijo*aAmapN , which is sometimes used; [but in the TA, miToraAbapN and miTowaAEapN and miqodaAmapN also are mentioned;] the p in mEzAbp , he says, is added to give intensiveness to the signification, and to imply praise; the meaning being, in his opinion, a man who frequently betakes himself, with his cattle, or camels &c., pasturing at a distance from others, to the places where rain has fallen, and to the uncropped herbage produced thereby; and he adds that the p is affixed to a masc. epithet to imply praise or blame when intensiveness is meant. (TA.) The two epithets above are also expl. as applied to a man who pastures his camels at a distance from the abode of the tribe, not repairing to them to rest. (TA.) [See also EazabN &c.] ― -b2- Also, (S, O, K, TA,) or ↓ miEozaAbN , (A, TA,) (tropical:) A man who has been long without a wife, (S, A, O, K, TA,) so that he has no need of one. (TA.) ― -b3- See also EazabN

sourceDefinition: , [aor. ,] inf. n. EiZamN (S, Msb, K) and EaZaAmapN , (Msb, K,) accord. to El-Isbahánee, primarily signifies He was, or became, great in his bone: then metaphorically said of anything kabiyr [or great], whether an object of sense or of intel-lect, a substance or an accident: (TA:) i. q. kabura , (S, TA,) said of a thing [as meaning it was, or became, great, big, or large ], (S, Msb, TA,) in length and breadth and thickness: (TA:) [and in like manner, metaphorically, said of an object of intellect; meaning it was, or became, great in estimation or rank or dignity; and thus also said of a man: or it imports more than kabura ; signifying it was, or became, great in comparison with other things of its kind; huge, enormous, or vast; and in a similar sense it is said of a man; and in an incomparably higher sense, of God: (see EaZiymN , below:)] and ↓ AEZm said of an affair, or event, signifies [like EaZuma ] it became EaZiym . (TA.) EiZamN is the contr. of SigarN . (K.) ― -b2- EaZuma Einodahu , and EaZuma Ealayohi : see 6, in three places: and see also 4. And maA yaEoZumuniY [which is similar in meaning to mA yaEoZumu EalaY~a if not a mistranscription for mA yuEoZimuniY ]: see 4. ― -b3- In the case of expressing wonder, one says, EuZoma AlbaTonu baTonuka [ How great is the belly, thy belly ! ], contracting EaZuma , and transferring the vowel of its middle letter to [the place of] its first; and thus one does in the case of that which denotes praise or blame, and of whatever [verb] may be well used in the manner of niEoma , and biy^osa : but what may not be thus used does not admit of the transferring, though it may be contracted; so that you may say, Hasuna Alwajohu wajohuka and Hasona Alwajohu wajohuka and Husona Alwajohu wajohuka , but not qado Husona Alwajohu wajohuka . (S.) -A2- EaZama Alkaloba , inf. n. EaZomN , He gave the dog a bone to eat; as also ↓ AEZmhu . (K.) ― -b2- And EaZama fulaAnFA , inf. n. EaZamapN (K, TA) and EaZamN , (TA,) He struck such a one upon his bones. (K, TA.)

sourceDefinition: The qaSab [here meaning bone, but properly applied to the bones of the hands and feet, or of the arms and legs,] of an animal, upon which is the flesh: (K:) [dim. ↓ EuZayomN :] pl. definition: Self-magnification, pride, haughtiness, or insolence;
sourceDefinition: Self-magnification, pride, haughtiness, or insolence; (S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ EuZomN (S, K) and ↓ EuZ~aAmapN and ↓ EaZamuwtN : (K:) as an attribute of a human being, it is [generally] blamable: (Az, K, TA:) [but] one says, lifulaAni EaZamapN Einoda Aln~aAsi meaning To such a one belongs a title to honour, or respect, in the estimation of men; and ↓ lahu taEaAZumN likewise: and ↓ A_in~ahu laEaZiymu AlmaEaAZimi i. e. Verily he is great in respect of the title that he has to honour, and of the rights that are held in high account; one to whom it is incumbent [ on others ] to pay regard, or consideration. (TA.) ― -b2- As an attribute of God, it is not to be ascribed to a human being; (Az, K, TA;) for, in relation to Him [it means Incomparable greatness or majesty, and] it is not to be specified by the ascription of its quality, nor defined, nor likened to anything. (TA.) ― -b3- Also The thick part of the fore arm; (S;) the half next the elbow, of the fore arm, in which is the [ main ] muscle; the half next the hand being called the A^asalap . (Lh, K.) ― -b4- And The thick part of the tongue, (K, TA,) above the Eakadap , which is the root thereof. (TA.) ― -b5- EaZamaAtu Alqawomi The chiefs, and nobles, of the people, or party. (K, * TA.) ― -b6- See also A_iEoZaAmapN .

definition: Having the quality denoted by the verb EaZuma ;
sourceDefinition: Having the quality denoted by the verb EaZuma ; [i. e. great, big, or large; &c.;] (S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ EuZaAmN (S, K, TA) in an intensive sense [i. e. signifying very great &c.], (TA,) and ↓ EuZ~aAmN (K, TA) in a more intensive sense than EuZaAmN [i. e. signifying very very great &c.]: (TA:) or EaZiymN signifies esteemed great &c. by another or others; differing from kabiyrN , which signifies “ great &c. in itself: ” (El-Fakhr Er-Rázee, TA:) or the former is the contr. of HaqiyrN ; [i. e. it signifies of great account or estimation; ] and as HaqiyrN is inferior to SagiyrN , so EaZiymN is superior to kabiyrN ; (Ksh and Bd in ii. 6;) and signifies great, or the like, in comparison with other things of its kind: (Bd ibid:) [it may therefore often be rendered huge, enormous, or vast: used metaphorically, as applied to an object of the intellect, it means great in estimation or rank or dignity; and thus as applied to a man: also of great magnitude or moment or importance: of great gravity: difficult, hard, severe, grievous, distressing, afflictive, troublesome, or burdensome: (see 6:) and formidable, or terrible. (Bd in xxii. 1.) Hence one says, rajulN EaZiymN fiY Almajodi waAlr~aA^oYi (tropical:) [ A man great in respect of glory, honour, dignity, or nobility, and of judgment, or opinion ]. (TA.) And ramaAhu biEaZiymK and ↓ bimuEoZamK (assumed tropical:) [ He reproached him, or upbraided him, with, or he accused him of, a thing, or an act, of great gravity; or an enormity ]: both mean the same. (TA.) [The pl. of EaZiymN is EiZaAmN and, applied to rational beings, EuZamaA='u .] ― -b2- AlEaZiymu as an epithet applied to God is syn. with Alkabiyru [signifying The Incomparably-great ]. (TA.)

definition: , inf. n. EilaAjN (S, A, O, K) and muEaAlajapN , (S, O, K,) He laboured, exerted himself, strove, struggled, contended, or conflicted, with it, (namely, a thing, S, O,) to prevail, overcome, or gain...
sourceDefinition: , inf. n. EilaAjN (S, A, O, K) and muEaAlajapN , (S, O, K,) He laboured, exerted himself, strove, struggled, contended, or conflicted, with it, (namely, a thing, S, O,) to prevail, overcome, or gain the mastery or possession, or to effect an object; he worked, or laboured, at it, or upon it, to do, execute, perform, effect, or accomplish, it, or to manage, or treat, it; syn. zaAwalahu ; (S, A, O, K;) and maArasahu . (TA.) [And He exercised his skill upon it; worked, or wrought, it; worked it together; mingled, mixed up, or compounded, it, with some degree of labour; mashed it; kneaded it; manipulated it; brewed it; treated it with some admixture; dressed it, or prepared it for use; namely, some substance, composition, food, medicine, or the like.] mino kasobihi waEilaAjihi is a phrase occurring in a trad., meaning From his gain, or earning, and his work, or labour. (L.) And one says, EAlj AlHadiyda He worked, or wrought, iron. (L in art. Hd , &c.) And EAlj furu$FA wawasaAy^ida [ He manufactured beds, or the like, and pillows ]. (K in art. njd .) And EAlj Al$~araAba biAln~aAri [ He brewed, or prepared with pains, the beverage, or wine, by means of fire; or boiled it well ]. (K voce muSaE~adN .) And EAlj Als~iHora [ He wrought enchantment ]. (K in art. twl .) And EaAlajonaA gayoba Als~amaA='i [ We laboured, or strove, after the secrets of heaven ]. (K in art. lms .) ― -b2- Also He laboured, or strove, with him, to prevail, or overcome; syn. zaAwalahu . (L.) One says, EaAlajahu ↓ faEalajahu , (S, O, * L, K, *) [aor. of the latter ,] inf. n. EalojN , (S,) He laboured, or strove, with him, to prevail, or overcome, (L,) and he overcame him (S, O, L, K) in so doing; (O, K;) namely, another man. (S, O.) It is said in a trad., EaAlajotu A@moraA^apF faA^aSabotu minohaA [ I strove with a woman, and obtained what I desired of her ]. (L.) And lamo yuEaAlijo , in another trad., is said to mean He did not strive, or contend, with the confusion of intel-lect [ usually ] attendant upon death, which would be an expiation for [some of] his sins: or he did not strive, or contend, with the severity of longcontinued sickness, nor suffer the perturbation [ usually ] attending death: or, as some relate it, the phrase is lamo yuEaAlajo , meaning he was not tended, or treated medically, in his sickness. (L.) In another trad. occurs the saying, A_in~iY SaAHibu ZahorK A^uEaAlijuhu , meaning Verily I am the owner of a camel for riding or carriage, which I ply, or work, ( A^umaArisuhu ,) and employ to carry for hire. (L.) And it is related in another trad. that 'Alee sent two men in a certain direction, and said, A_in~akumaA EilojaAni faEaAlijaA Eano diynikumaA , meaning Verily ye are two strong, bulky men, therefore labour ye [ in defence of your religion ] in the affair to the performance of which I have called and incited you. (L.) ― -b3- [And He plied it; i. e. kept it at work, or in action; namely, a thing. See an ex. voce dulobN .] ― -b4- Also, (O, K,) inf. ns. as above, [but generally EilaAjN ,] (K,) He treated him (i. e. a person either sick or wounded, or a beast, O) medically, curatively, or therapeutically: (O, K:) he tended him, or took care of him, in his sickness: (L:) [ he endeavoured to cure him (i. e. a sick person), or it (i. e. a diseased part of the body):] and EAljhu mina Ald~aA='i , inf. n. EilaAjN , he treated him medically to cure him of the disease. (MA.) [And He dressed it, namely, a wound or the like.] And one says, Euwlijati Als~ibaAEu biA^uxa*K , meaning The beasts, or birds, of prey were wrought upon, or operated on, by charms, so as to prevent their injuring cattle and the like. (L in art. Eqd .)

sourceDefinition: is said of a man's make [as meaning It was, or became, strong, or sturdy, and big, or bulky ]: (A:) [or] it was, or became, thick, big, or coarse. (Kh, O.) definition: (S, O, L, K) and ↓ EalajN (L, TA) A certain sort of plant;
sourceDefinition: (S, O, L, K) and ↓ EalajN (L, TA) A certain sort of plant; (S, O, K;) growing in the sand: n. un. with p : (O:) AHn says, on the authority of certain of the Arabs of the desert, that it grows in the form of slender strings, intensely green, of a greenness like that of herbs, or leguminous plants, inclining to yellowness, bare, having no leaves: (O:) he says [also] that the Ealaj [or EalajaAn , as will be shown by what follows,] is, with the people of Nejd, a sort of trees [or shrubs ] having no leaves, consisting only of bare strings, of a dusty green colour: (L, TA:) the asses eat it, and their teeth become yellow in consequence of their eating it; wherefore one says of him who has yellow teeth, kaA^an~a faAhu fuw HimaArK A^akala EalajaAnFA [ As though his mouth were the mouth of an ass that had eaten 'alaján; by the mouth being meant the teeth, as is often the case]: (O, L, TA:) and he says that it sometimes grows, not in the sand, but in soft, or plain, tracts; and accord. to some, (O,) the EalajaAn is a sort of trees of a dark green colour, not having leaves, consisting only of twigs, one of such trees occupying the space of a man sitting; (O, L, TA; *) growing in plain, or soft, land, and not eaten by the camels unless of necessity: Az says that the EalajaAn is a sort of trees resembling that called EalanodFY , which he had seen in the desert: and its pl. [or rather the pl. of the n. un. ( EalajapN ) of its syn. ↓ EalajN ] is EalajaAtN . (L, TA.)

sourceDefinition: A she-goat; the female of the common goat: (S, O, K:) or a she-goat a year old; (Msb;) [and so ↓ EanozapN : (Freytag, from the Kitáb el-Addád:)] and the female of the mountain-goat; and of the gazelle: (S, O:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aEonuzN and [of mult.] EunuwzN and EinaAzN , or, accord, to some, the last of these is pl. of EanozN in the last of the senses expl. above. (TA.) humaA karukobataYi AlEanozi [ They two are like the two knees of the she-goat ] is a prov. applied to two men vying with each other, (O, K,) or equalling each other, (TA,) because her two knees, when she desires to lie down, fall together. (O, K. [See Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 861: where, instead of AlEnz , we find AlbaEiyri ; and thus I find in a MS. copy of the Proverbs of Meyd.]) And it is said in another prov., to him who commits a crime that occasions his destruction, laA taku kaA@loEanozi taboHavu Eani Almudoyapi [ Be not thou like the she-goat that scrapes up the dust, or earth, from over the butcher's knife ]. (TA. [See also baAHivN .]) Hence the saying, yawomN kayawomi AlEanozi [ A day like the day of the she-goat ]; mentioned by Th; alluding to its bringing death. (TA.) And laqiYa yawoma AlEanozi [ He met with the day of the she-goat ] is also a prov., (O, TA,) applied to him who meets with that which destroys him, (O, K,) or to him who labours for his own destruction. (A.) ― -b2- AlEanozu is a name of (assumed tropical:) The star [ ε ] on the left [or (as some figure the constellation) the right ] elbow of Auriga: and AlEinaAzu is a name of (assumed tropical:) The two stars [ ζ and η ] on the left [or the right ] wrist together with AlEay~uwq [which is Capella ]. (Kzw in his description of Auriga.) ― -b3- Also The female eagle: (S, O, K: [see also EanosN :]) pl. EunuwzN . (TA.) And The female vulture: (IDrd, O, K:) pl. EunuwzN . (IDrd, O.) And The female of the [ species of bustard called ] HubAraY (IDrd, O, K) is sometimes thus termed: (O:) and it is said to be also called ↓ AlEanozapu . (TA.) And The female of the hawk. (TA.) ― -b4- Also A species of aquatic bird; (O, K; *) [by some, in the present day, applied to a gray heron; ] also called Eanozu AlmaA='i . (O.) ― -b5- And A species of fish; also called EanozuAlmaA='i : (Az, O:) accord. to Ibn- 'Abbád, (O,) a certain great fish, which a mule can hardly, or in nowise, carry: (O, K:) and the pl., he says, is A^aEonizapN . (O.) -A2- EanozN also signifies An [ eminence, or a hill, such as is termed ] A^akamap : (S:) or a black A^akamap . (O, K.) ― -b2- And A rock in the water: pl. EunuwzN . (TA.) ― -b3- And Land having in it ruggedness and sand and stones and [ the species of tamarisk called ] A^avol . (TA.) -A3- And I. q. baATilN [q. v.]. (TA.)
