sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. farosN , (S, M, O, Msb, K, &c.,) He (a lion) broke, or crushed so as to break, its neck; (S, A, * Mgh, * O, K;) i. e., the neck of his fariysap ; (S, O, K;) as also ↓ Aftrshu : (S:) this is the primary signification: (S, Mgh, TA:) or he (a beast of prey) seized it, (a thing,) and broke, or crushed so as to break, its neck; as also ↓ Aftrshu : (M:) or he (a lion) broke it; i. e., his fariysap : (Msb:) and he bruised, or crushed, and broke, it; namely, a thing. (M.) Accord. to ISk, (S,) you say, faras Al*iy^obu Al$~aApa , (S, TA,) meaning The wolf seized the sheep, or goat, and broke, or crushed so as to break, its neck: (TA:) accord. to En-Nadr (i. e. ISh), you say, A^akala Al*~iy^obu Al$~aApa [The wolf ate, or devoured, the sheep, or goat], but not ↓ AftrshA . (S, O, TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (S, Mgh, O, Msb,) He killed it, in any manner; (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K;) as also ↓ Aftrshu : (TA:) or ↓ the latter, he (a lion, O, or a wolf, TA) captured it; or made it his prey. (O, K, TA. See also 2 [where a similar but tropical usage of the former verb is mentioned.]) You say, farasahu AlA^asadu The lion killed him or it. (Mgh.) ― -b3- farasa Al*~abiyHapa , (M, Msb,) aor. , (M,) inf. n. as above, (S, M, Mgh,) He (the slaughterer) broke the bone of the neck of the slaughtered animal before it became cold: (S, Mgh, O:) or broke its neck before its death: (Msb:) or cut, or severed, its nuxaAE [or spinal cord ]: or divided its neck: (M, TA:) or slaughtered it so as to reach to the nxAE : (AO, TA:) the action thus [variously] expl. is forbidden. (S, Mgh, Msb, TA.) ― -b4- qabiyHapF ↓ farasahu firosapF He struck him [ in an abominable manner, app. in the back, ] so that the part between his hips became depressed and his navel protruded. (M.) -A2- farusa , aor. , (S, A, O, K,) inf. n. furuwsapN (S, A, O, K *) and faraAsapN (S, K, * in the O firaAsapN ) and furuwsiy~apN , (S, * A, O, * K, *) all of which ns. are mentioned as syn. by As, (TA,) [as they are also in the S and K,] and the first and last, in like manner, by IAar, (TA,) [but the first is expressly said to be an inf. n. of farusa in the S and A only, and the second in the S only, and the third (which seems to be rather a simple subst.) in the A only,] He was, or became, skilled in horsemanship, or in the management of horses, (S, A, O, K, TA,) and in riding them, (O, * K, TA,) and in urging them to run, and in remaining firm upon them: (TA:) or faraAsapN and furuwsapN are inf. ns. having no verb: Lh only [says ISd] mentions farasa and farusa as signifying he became a horseman; and this is extr.: (M, TA:) but [beside what has been cited above, from the S and A and K,] IKtt also says that farasa Alxayola , inf. n. furuwsapN and furuwsiy~apN , signifies he rode horses well; and in like manner farusa [but not followed by Alxyl ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (assumed tropical:) He was, or became, skilled in anything that he endeavoured to do. (TA.) -A3- farasa biAln~aZari , [and binaZarihi , and biEayonihi , and farasa fiY Aln~aAsi , (see faArisN ,)] aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. firaAsapN and faraAsapN , (As, IAar, Msb, TA,) accord. to the citation of the words of As and IAar in the L, but this is at variance with the opinion generally held, [which is, that faraAsapN is an inf. n. only of farusa , signifying as expl. above, and that firaAsapN is a subst. from tafar~usN , having no proper verb of which it is an inf. n.,] (TA,) is said of a man [in the same sense as tafar~asa , (q. v.,) as will be seen from the explanations of firaAsapN and faArisN , below]. (Msb.) See 5, latter part, in two places. -A4- farisa He kept continually, or constantly, to the eating of the dates called faraAs . (O, K.) ― -b2- And He pastured upon, or depastured, the plants called firos . (O, K.)

(M, TA.) -A2- fr~sh Al$~aYo'a , (inf. n. as above, TA,) He exposed to him (namely a wild beast) the thing, [meaning the animal,] that he might seize it, and break, or crush so as to break, its neck: and A_ay~aAhu ↓ A^aforasahu the threw, or cast, it to him, that he might do so to it: (M:) and Alr~ajulu AlA^asada HimaArahu ↓ A^aforasa the man left his ass to the lion, that he might break his neck, or kill him, or make him his prey, while he himself should escape. (S, K.) El-'Ajjáj uses the former verb in relation to the kind of flies called nuEar , saying, DarobFA A_i*aA SaAba AlyaA=fiyxa A@Hotafaro fiY AlhaAmi duHolaAnFA yufar~isona Aln~uEaro [ A beating which, when it falls upon the tops of heads, digs, in the pates, hollows that afford prey to the blue stinging flies ]; meaning, that these wounds are wide, and enable the nEr to obtain thence what they desire. (M.) And one of the poets uses it in relation to human beings, in the following verses, [which exhibit an instance of the license termed A_iqowaA=' ,] cited by IAar: qado A^arosaluwniY qiY AlkawaAEibi raAEiyFA ↓ faqado waA^abiY raAEiY AlkawaAEibi A^uforasu A^atatohu *iy^aAbN laA yubaAliyna raAEiyFA wakun~u sawaAmFA ta$otahiY A^ano tufar~asaA [ They had sent me among the girls with swelling breasts, as a guardian; and, by my father, while guardian of the girls with swelling breasts, or by the father of the guardian of the girls with swelling breasts, I was (lit. I am ) made a prey: there came thither wolves not caring for a guardian, and those females were (as) pasturing camels eagerly desiring to be given as prey ]: he likens these women to pasturing camels, although differing from them inasmuch as the latter do not eagerly desire to be given as prey, since this would be a cause of their death, whereas women do eagerly desire it, since farosu Alr~ijaAli liln~isaA='i [lit. men's making women their prey ] is in this case (assumed tropical:) men's holding commerce of love with women: A^uforasu is for furisotu ; for, as Sb says, they sometimes put A^afoEalu in the place of faEalotu : A^abiY is in the gen. case as governed by wa denoting swearing; and rAEY AlkwAEb may be a denotative of state relating to the t [the pronoun of the first person] understood [in A^uforasu for furisotu ]; or wA^bY may be prefixed to rAEY AlkwAEb , governing it in the gen. case, and by the latter expression he may mean himself: by wolves not caring for a guardian, he means wicked men not caring for him who guarded these women: and he uses the word t$thY to denote intense desire; for if he did not mean intenseness, he would have said turiydu . (M.)

sourceDefinition: He pretended to others that he was a horseman, or one skilled in horsemanship. (As, O, K.) -A2- He acted deliberately, (S, O, K, TA,) and considered, or examined, a thing, or did so repeatedly, in order to know it, or to obtain a clear knowledge of it. (M.) You say, tafar~asotu fiyhi xayorFA , (S, O,) or Alxayora , (Msb,) [ I perceived in him good, or goodness, intuitively; &c.: or] I discovered ( taEar~afotu ) in him good, or goodness, by right opinion. (Msb.) sourceDefinition: [ A horse; and a mare; ] one of what are called xayolN ; (M;) the name frs is given to it because it crushes and breaks the ground with its hoofs; (A, O; *) and is applied to the male and the female; (S, M, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K;) but mostly applied to the latter; (M;) the female not being called ↓ farasapN ; (S, O;) or the female is [sometimes] thus called: (Yoo, IJ, M, Msb, K:) it is applied also to the Arabian, (Mgh, Msb,) and to the Turkish, (Msb,) or that which is not Arabian: (Mgh:) or, accord. to Mohammad [the Hanafee Imám], to the Arabian only; but for this [says Mtr] I find no authority of a lexicologist, except that ISk, speaking of a solid-hoofed animal, says, “ whether it be a birozawon or a faras or a bagol or a HimaAr : ” (Mgh:) the pl. is A^aforaAsN , (S, M, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) [a pl. of pauc. but used as a pl. of mult. also,] and A^aforusN , [a pl. of pauc. only,] (O,) and furuwsN : (K:) and as farasN is originally fem., you say valaAvu A^aforaAsK when you mean males [as well as when you mean females]: (M:) or you say valaAvapu A^aforaAsK , with p , when you mean males; and valaAvu A^aforaAsK , without p , when you mean females: (Msb:) the dim. is furayosN , (S, O, Msb,) when applied to the male; (Msb;) and ↓ furayosapN , when applied to the female; (S, O, Msb;) agreeably with rule; (Msb;) accord. to Aboo-Bekr Ibn-Es-Sarráj: (S, O:) or ↓ furayosN when applied to the female [also], which is extr. (Sb, M. [See HarobN .]) ― -b2- humaA kafarasaYo rihaAnK [ They two are like two horses running for a wager ] is a saying applied to two persons running a race to a goal, and being equal: (A, O, K:) the comparison relating to the beginning [of a contest], for the termination necessarily shows which outstrips; (O, K:) and to two who are equal, and two who are nearly equal, in excellence &c. (Har p. 640.) It was said by a man who swore that he would abstain from his wife for four months, and then divorced her: for the period during which a woman may be taken back after a [first or second] divorce is that of three menstruations or three periods of purity from menstruation; and if it ended in this case before the end of the four months during which he swore to abstain from her, she became separated from him by that divorcement: so he likened the two periods to two horses running for a wager. (O, * TA.) ― -b3- farasu AlbaHori (assumed tropical:) [ The horse of the great river; i. e., of the Nile;] the hippopotamus. (Dmr. [See also EaSobN .]) ― -b4- Alfarasu (assumed tropical:) A well-known constellation; so called because of its resemblance in form to a horse; (M;) [i. e.] Alfarasu AlA^aEoZamu (assumed tropical:) [ The Greater, or Greatest, Horse; ] the constellation Pegasus. (Kzw.) ― -b5- qiToEapu Alfarasi (assumed tropical:) [ The Piece of the Horse; ] the constellation Equuleus. (Kzw.) ― -b6- Alfarasu Alt~aAm~u (assumed tropical:) [ The Complete horse; ] a certain constellation composed of thirty-one stars, in which a portion of the constellation called Alfarasu AlA^aEoZamu is included. (Kzw. [It is further described by him; but in a manner that does not enable me to identify it with any of the constellations named by our astronomers.])

sourceDefinition: , (IAar, S, M, O, K, TA,) or ↓ Alfirosapu , (M, TA,) the former accord. to A'Obeyd, (M, TA,) or, accord. to A'Obeyd, it is with S , and the vulgar, he says, pronounce it with s , (O,) Gibbosity [ of the back ]; syn. AlHadabu : (IAar, O, TA:) or, (M, O, K, TA,) as also AlfaroSapu , (M, O,) which latter is the more approved in this sense, (M,) the riyH [or flatus ] of gibbosity; (M, O, K, TA;) [i. e.] the ryH that renders gibbous; (M;) as though it were breaking, or crushing so as to break, the back ( kaA^an~ahaA taforisu AlZ~ahora A^aYo taduq~uhu ), and cleaving it ( taforiSuhu A^aYo ta$uq~uhu ): (O:) [or Alfarosapu signifies the displacement of one of the vertebræ; for,] accord. to As, one says A^aSaAbatohu farosapN when one of the vertebræ of one's back has become displaced; but the flatus ( Alr~iyHu ) from which gibbosity results is termed AlfaroSapu , with S : (TA:) or Alfarosapu signifies a flatus that attacks in the neck, and breaks it: (S:) or, as some say, an imposthume, or ulcer, ( qaroHap ,) that is in the neck, breaking it: (M:) or a breach ( furojap ) in the neck; thus says AZ: or a breach ( frjp ) that is in [ the case of ] gibbosity: the pl. is farasaAtN , not A^aforisapN , which latter is said to be a pl. of farosapN , but is anomalous. (K.)

sourceDefinition: , accord. to Er-Rághib, primarily signifies Alt~aforiyju [i. e. The opening a thing; and particularly by diduction, or so as to form an intervening space, or a gap, or breach ]. (TA.) You say, fak~a , first pers. fakakotu , (S, O, Msb, K,) aor. , inf. n. fak~N , (O, Msb,) He separated (S, O, Msb, K) a thing (S, O, K) from another thing; and any two things knit together, or intricately intermixed: (S, O:) or fakakotuhu I separated one part of it from another part thereof: (Msb:) and ↓ tafokiykN likewise signifies the separating two things knit together, or intricately intermixed. (Lth, S, TA.) And He broke [or broke open ] a seal, i. e. a sealed piece of clay or wax; (Mgh, Msb, * TA;) in relation to which ↓ yafotak~uhu occurs as meaning yafuk~uhu , though we have not heard it [as a classical expression in this sense]. (Mgh.) ― -b2- And fak~a AlEaZoma , (Mgh, Msb,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (Msb,) He dislocated the bone; put it out of joint. (Mgh, Msb.) [This, or the like, is what is meant by its being said that] Alfak~u in the hand, or arm, is [i. e. denotes] less than Alkasoru . (K.) ― -b3- And fak~a yadahu , (K, TA,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (TA,) He opened, or unclosed, his hand from what was in it: (K, TA:) so in the M. (TA.) ― -b4- And fak~a Alr~ahona , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. fak~N and fukuwkN ; (K;) and ↓ Aftk~hu ; (S, Mgh, O, K;) (tropical:) He redeemed the pledge; (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K, TA;) got it out from the hand of him to whom it was pledged. (Mgh.) ― -b5- And fakakotu signifies also I loosed, set loose or free, or let go, anything. (Msb.) ― -b6- [Hence,] fak~a AlA^asiyru , (Msb, K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. fak~N and fakaAkN and fikaAkN , (K,) (tropical:) He liberated, or set free, the captive. (Msb, K, TA.) And fak~a Alr~aqabapa , (S, O, Msb, K,) aor. , inf. n. fak~N , (TA,) [lit. He loosed the neck, ] means (tropical:) he emancipated [ the slave ]. (S, O, Msb, K, TA.) fak~u Alr~aqabapi is expl. in a trad. as meaning (assumed tropical:) The assisting in paying the price [ of the slave when one is unable to pay the whole of the price]. (O, TA.) In the Kur [xc. 13], fak~u raqabapK is said by some to mean (assumed tropical:) The emancipating of a slave: and by some. (assumed tropical:) the man's emancipating himself from subjection to God's punishment by the confession of the unity of God and by righteous doing and then by teaching the same to others. (TA,) fuk~a fulaAnN means (assumed tropical:) Such a one was set free, and at rest, from a thing. (IAar, Th, TA.) ― -b7- [Hence also,] one says, huwa yafuk~u Alma$aAkila (assumed tropical:) [ He solves ] the things, or affairs, that are dubious, or confused. (TA in art. $kl .) ― -b8- qadofak~a wafar~aja is said of a very old man, meaning far~aja laHoyayohi [i. e. He has parted his jaws, by hanging the lower jaw in consequence of weakness]; as is the case in extreme old age. (S, O,) And [hence.] fak~a , (AZ, S, O, K,) aor. , inf. n. fak~N and fukuwkN , (AZ, S, O,) said of a man, means (assumed tropical:) He was, or became, extremely aged, or old and weak. (AZ, S, O, K.) [Or fak~a thus used may be from Alfak~u signifying “ the jaw: ” and so what next follows.] ― -b9- fakakotu AlS~abiY~a I put medicine into the mouth of the boy or young male child [opening his jaws for that purpose]. (S, O.) -A2- qado fakikota , [third pers. fak~a ,] aor. tafak~u , inf. n. fakakN , Thou hast become such as is termed A^afak~u i. e. one whose manokib [here meaning shoulder-bone ] has become unknit, or loosened, ( Ainofaraja ,) from its joint, in consequence of weakness and flaccidity. (S.) [See also fakakN below.] ― -b2- And qadofakikota , aor. tafak~u ; (S, O, K;) and fakukota , (O, K,) a verb of a very rare form, [respecting which see dam~a , last sentence,] (MF, TA,) aor. tafuk~u ; (O, K;) inf. n. fak~apN (S, O, K) and fak~N also; (TA;) (tropical:) Thou hast become foolish, or stupid, and soft, flaccid, or languid. (S, O, K, TA.)

definition: The laHoY [meaning jaw;
sourceDefinition: The laHoY [meaning jaw; and also either of the two lateral portions of the lower jaw ], (S, O, Msb, K,) i. e. (Msb) each of the laHoyaAni ; (Mgh, Msb;) as also ↓ AlA^afak~u : (O, K:) or this latter signifies the majomaE [or part in which is the commissure ] of the xaTom [generally meaning muzzle ]; (Lth, O, K;) as also Alfak~u ; (TA;) that is, (Lth, O, in the K “ or ” [as if to denote a different meaning],) [ the part in which is the symphysis ] of the fak~aAni [or two lateral portions of the lower jaw ]: (Lth, O, K:) [see Alfaniyku :] and Alfak~aAni is said to mean the place [ on either side with that on the other side ] where the two jaws meet [ and are articulated ] next the temple, above and below; of a human being and of a horse or the like: (TA:) and, in the Bári', (Msb,) or in the T, (TA,) the place of meeting of the two sides of the mouth ( mulotaqaY Al$~idoqayoni ) on both sides: (Msb, TA:) [but this last explanation is strange, and app. little known:]) pl. fukuwkN . (Msb.) One says, maqotalu Alr~ajuli bayona fak~ayohi [which may be best rendered The man's slayer is between his two jaws, or two lateral portions of his lower jaw ]; (S, O, TA;) meaning the man's tongue: (TA:) a prov., in which mqtl may be [properly] an inf. n., or a noun of place, or an inf. n. used in the place of an act. part. n.: accord. to the third of these explanations, [which most nearly denotes the meaning intended,] it is as though one said, qaAtilu Alr~ajuli bayona fak~ayohi . (Meyd. [See Freytag's Arab. Prov., ii. 597.]) See also fakakN .

sourceDefinition: in the Kur [xcviii. 1], (O, TA,) followed by the words Hat~aY taA^otiyahumu A@lobay~inapu , (O,) means, accord. to Mujáhid (O, TA) and Zj, (TA,) In the condition of desisting (O, TA) from their infidelity; (TA;) or, as Akh says, ceasing from their infidelity: (TA:) or, accord. to another, (O,) namely, Niftaweyh, (TA,) quitting the present state of existence, (O, TA,) i. e., sharing, one with another, in perdition, until the evidence came to them (O, TA) that had been affirmed to them in the Towráh, with respect to the description of Mohammad &c.; taA^otiyahum being lit. an aor., but in its meaning a pret.: (O:) Az says that it is not from maA A@nofak~a meaning maA zaAla , but from AinofikaAku Al$~aYo'i mina Al$~aYo'i meaning “ the thing's becoming separated from the thing: ” accord. to IAar, as mentioned by Th, fuk~a fulaAnN means “ Such a one was set free, and at rest, from a thing; ” and hence mnfk~yn in the Kur means experiencing rest: accord. to Er-Rághib, it means separated, or separated into several parties; for all [to whom the word, preceded by a negative, relates] were assenting to error. sourceDefinition: , [aor. , (TK,)] inf. n. funuwkN , He remained, stayed, dwelt, or abode, in the place. (El-Umawee, S, O, K.) ― -b2- fanaka fiY AlA^amori , (S, O, K, *) aor. as above, (S,) and so the inf. n., (S, O,) He persisted, or persevered, in the affair; (S, O, K; *) as also ↓ Afnk . (K.) [See also fataka ; and see other explanations below.] And fanaka fiY Alka*ibi He persisted, or persevered, in lying: asserted by Yaakoob to be formed by transposition from fakana : and Aboo-Tálib says that ↓ fAnk and ↓ fn~k , of which latter the inf. n. is tafoniykN , signify he persisted, or persevered, in lying, and in evil; not in good; and denote the like of consecutiveness. (TA.) [See also fanokN , which may be an inf. n. of fanaka in this sense, and in others.] And fanaka Ealayohi , (K, TA,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) signifies [in like manner] He kept, or applied himself, constantly, perseveringly, or assiduously, to it; as also ↓ Afnk . (K, TA.) ― -b3- And fanaka fiY AlT~aEaAmi , (Ibn-'Abbád, S, O, K,) aor. as above, (S,) and so the inf. n., (S, O,) He continued constantly, uniformly, or regularly, in the eating of the food, not loathing aught thereof; (Ibn-'Abbád, S, O, K;) as also fanika , (S, O, K,) with kesr, (S, O,) like Ealima , (K,) inf. n. funuwkN ; (S, O, K;) and so ↓ fAnk : (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K:) and AlT~aEaAma ↓ faAnakotu waAl$~araAba signifies [simply] I kept continually, or constantly, to the food and the beverage: and also I loathed them, or turned away from them with disgust. (Ibn-'Abbád, O.) ― -b4- And fanaka fiY AlA^amori [not fAnk as in the lexicons of Golius and Freytag, the latter of whom gives both forms of the v. in the sense here following, as does also the TK,] signifies also He entered into the affair. (K.) ― -b5- And He mastered the affair, and overcame it. (O.) ― -b6- fanakota fiY lawomiY , and fyh ↓ Afnkt , (both in the TA, but the latter only in the O,) Thou wast, or hast become, skilled in the blaming, or censuring, of me, and profuse, or immoderate, therein: so says Fr. (O, TA.) ― -b7- And fanakato and ↓ A^afonakato She (a woman) blamed, or censured, and kept continually, or constantly, to blaming, or censuring, or to some other thing [or act ]. (Lth, O, TA. *) ― -b8- And the former, said of a girl, or young woman, She cared not for what she did nor for what was said to her. (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K.) This meaning has also been assigned to fatakato . (TA.) ― -b9- And fanaka , (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) He lied, or said what was untrue; as also ↓ Afnk . (K.)

definition: A certain beast, (Kr, O, K,) of the skin of which the furred garment is made;
sourceDefinition: A certain beast, (Kr, O, K,) of the skin of which the furred garment is made; (Kr, S, O;) [the marten; ] the furred garment whereof is the best sort of such garments, and the highest in estimation, and the most equable, and is suitable to all temperate constitutions: (K:) it is said to be a species of the Turkish fox's cubs; and therefore Az and others say that the word is arabicized; some of the travellers relate that it is applied to the young-one of the jackal ( Aibon A=waY ) in the country of the Turks: (Msb:) it is also said to mean a certain skin that is worn; and to be an arabicized word: [in Pers. a furred garment is called fanak :] IDrd says, “ I do not think it to be Arabic: ” and MF mentions ↓ faniykN as signifying an animal like the fox; an arabicized word; from [a work entitled] gaAyap AlbayaAn ; and he says that it appears to be the fanak that is mentioned in the K. (TA.) ― -b2- See also fanokN .

definition: The majomaE [or part in which is the symphysis ] of the laHoyaAni [or two lateral portions of the lower jaw ], (Lth, O, K, TA,) in the middle of the chin, (Lth, O, TA,) of a man;
sourceDefinition: The majomaE [or part in which is the symphysis ] of the laHoyaAni [or two lateral portions of the lower jaw ], (Lth, O, K, TA,) in the middle of the chin, (Lth, O, TA,) of a man; (Lth, O, K, TA;) this is when the word is used in the sing. form; (Lth, O; [see also Alfak~u ;]) and it is also called ↓ AlA_ifoniyku ; (Lth, O;) [and in like manner Aboo-'Amr Esh-Sheybánee explained what is meant by the upper faniyk as is stated by IF and in the O:] or the extremity [ of each ] of the laHoyaAni , at the place of the Eanofaqap [or tuft of hair that is between the lower lip and the chin; ] (S, K;) also called ↓ AlA_ifoniyku ; but Ks knew not this: (S:) or the faniykaAni are the two extremities of the Eanofaqap : (O:) or (K, TA, in the CK “ and ”) the sing. signifies a bone [ beneath the temple, ] to which the shaving of the head reaches ( EaZomN yanotahiY A_ilayohi Haloqu Alr~aA^osi ): (K, TA:) and accord. to Lth, the dual signifies the two extremities of the [ lower ] jaw, of whatever has a jaw, that move in the act of chewing, below the temples: (O:) or, accord. to Sh, the two thin, rising bones, [app. the two coronoid processes of the jaw, ] lower than the ears, between the temple and the ball of the cheek. (TA.) The lower faniyk is [app. The symphysis of the pubes; being] said by Aboo-'Amr Esh-Sheybánee to be the part where the two hip-bones meet together: (IF, O:) [hence, perhaps, and therefore it may be erroneously,] the fnyk is said by AA to be the root, or base, of the tail: (TA:) and it signifies, as also ↓ AlA_ifoniyku , (IDrd, O, K,) the zimik~aY , (K,) or zimij~aY , [i. e. the place of growth, or the root, or the whole, of the tail, of a bird, or] of a young bird; as they assert; (IDrd, O;) but IDrd says, “ I will not pronounce it to be correct: ” (O:) and the dual signifies two bones cleaving together: when, in the female pigeon, they are broken, she does not retain her eggs [ sufficiently ], but excludes them prematurely. (Lth, O.) -A2- See also fanakN .

sourceDefinition: , aor. yafuwzu , inf. n. fawozN (S, A, O, Msb, K) and mafaAzN and mafaAzapN , (TA,) He attained, acquired, gained, or won, good, or good fortune, (S, A, O, Msb, * K,) or his wish or desire, or what he desired or sought; (Bd in iii. 182, and TA;) he met with, or experienced, that for which one would be regarded with a wish to be in the like condition, without its being desired that it should pass away from him; he became far from what was disliked, or hated, or evil: (TA:) he succeeded, or was successful: he won, or gained the victory: (Msb:) [ he had his arrow drawn, or] his arrow came forth [ from the ribaAbap ], in the game called Almayosir : and (tropical:) it (an arrow) won; or came forth before its fellow [ or fellows in that game ]. definition: A place of safety, security, or escape.
sourceDefinition: A place of safety, security, or escape. (S, A, O, K.) So in the Kur [iii. 185], falaA taHosiban~ahumo bimafaAzapK mina AlEa*aAbi [ Do thou by no means reckon them to be in a place of security from punishment ]: (S, A, * O:) or, accord. to Fr, the meaning here is, far from punishment. (TA.) ― -b2- A cause, or means, of prosperity, or success, or of the attainment or acquisition of that which one desires or seeks, or of what is good, or of that whereby one becomes in a happy or good state; syn. mafolaHapN . (A.) ― -b3- (tropical:) [The state of temporary safety which is between the present life and that which is to come. See 1, last signification.] -A2- (tropical:) A place of perdition, or destruction: (Msb, K: *) or i. q. falaApN : (A:) [i. e.] a desert; syn. bar~iy~apN ; any [ desert such as is called ] qaforN : (TA:) or a desert in which is no water: (ISh, O, K:) and a desert in which is no water for the space of a journey of two nights or more: when there is none for the space of a journey of a night and a day, it is not thus called. (ISh, O, TA:) or a tract in which two wateringplaces are so far apart that camels are kept from drinking two days, with a portion of the day preceding them and of the day following them, [accord. to that which is generally preferred of the explanations of the term riboEN which is here employed,] and other animals [that journey quicker] drink on alternate days; as also falaApN : or such as is between that in which camels are kept from drinking two days &c. as above, and that in which other animals drink on alternate days; as also fayofaApN : (TA:) so called to prognosticate good fortune, and safety. (As, IF, S, A, O, Msb,) as meaning a place of safety, (A,) from faAza signifying “ he became safe: ” (Msb:) or from faw~aza , (IAar, S, O, * Msb,) or faAza . (AHei, TA.) signifying “ he perished, ” (IAar, S, O, * AHei,) or “ he died: ” (Msb, TA:) AHei condemns the former of these assertions; but Az and ISd say that it is the more commonly approved, though the latter is the more agreeable with analogy: (TA:) or it is so called because he who comes forth from it, having traversed it, is safe: (IAar, TA:) the pl. is mafaAwizu : (S:) and ↓ mafaAzN signifies the same as mafaAzapN . so in a trad. of Kaab Ibn-Málik; faA@sotaqobala safarFA baEiydFA wamafaAzFA [ And he saw before him, or looked forward to, a far journey and a desert, or a waterless desert, &c.]. (TA.)

definition: The twenty-first letter of the alphabet: called qaAfN .
sourceDefinition: The twenty-first letter of the alphabet: called qaAfN . Respecting its pronunciation as the title of the fiftieth chapter of the Kur-án, see SAd , in art. Swd . It is one of the letters termed majohuwrap [or vocal, i. e. pronounced with the voice, and not with the breath only]; its place of utterance is between the root of the tongue and the uvula, in the furthest part of the mouth; and it is of the strongest of the letters, and of the most certain of them in sound. (TA at the commencement of bAb AlqAf .) It is sometimes pronounced like the Pers. G , i. e. AlkaAfu Almamozuwjapu biAlqaAfi ; in which case it is termed AlqaAfu AlmaqoEuwdapu [?]: this mode of pronouncing it is well known as of the dial. of the people of El-Yemen [and others]: Ibn-Khaldoon says that it is of the dial. of Mudar; and that some of the people of the [Prophet's] house are so extravagant as to assert that recitation in prayer is not rightly but with this letter thus pronounced. (MF and TA voce jul~anaArN .) It has been substituted for one letter, i. e. k , [as some say,] in the instance of A^ukonapu AlT~aAy^iri [for which they sometimes said A^uqonap ]. (MF and TA at the commencement of bAb AlqAf . [It is there added that a pl. of A^ukonap has been heard, but not of A^uqonap , and this is a sign of the originality of the former: but A^uqanaAtN is mentioned as pl. of A^uqonap in art. Aqn in the TA.])

definition: A great number (AO, S, M, K) of men or people;
sourceDefinition: A great number (AO, S, M, K) of men or people; (S, K;) as also ↓ qaboSN : (M, TA:) thus applied it is like a dim. applied to that which is esteemed great. (El-Fáïk, O.) You say, A_in~ahumo lafiY qiboSi AlHaSaY Verily they are numerous as the pebbles. (TA.) And huwa fiY qiboSi AlHaSaY , and ↓ qaboSihaA , He is in, or among, a multitude that cannot be numbered. (O, TA.) [See also a verse of ElKumeyt cited in the first paragraph of art. vrw .] ― -b2- A place where a number is collected together of ants; as also ↓ qaboSN : (M:) and of bees; as also the latter word: (TA:) or where a great number of ants is collected together: (El-'Eyn, TA:) or where a great quantity of sand is collected together; as also the latter word. (Ibn-'Abbád, K.)

AiqotidaAdN ; (K;) He cut it in an enlongated form; or lengthwise: (IDrd, M, L, K:) or slit, split, clave, rent, or divided, it, (namely, a thong, &c., S, O, L, and a garment, or piece of cloth, L,) lengthwise: (S, M, A, O, L, Msb, K:) and he cut it off entirely: (M, L, K:) or he cut it, or cut it off, in an absolute sense: (TA:) he cut it, namely, a skin: and he rent it, namely, a garment, or piece of cloth, or the like. (L.) One says, Darabahu biAls~ayofi faqad~ahu biniSofayoni [ He smote him with the sword and clave him in halves, ] (L, Msb, *) or qad~ahu niSofayoni . (A.) And qad~a Alqalama waqaT~ahu [ He slit the writing-reed, and nibbed it, or cut off its point breadthwise, or crosswise ]: (A, TA:) [for] qaT~ahu is opposed to qad~ahu : (S and TA in art. qT :) and both of these verbs occur in a trad. describing 'Alee's different modes of cutting [with the sword] when contracting himself and when stretching himself up. (TA.) ― -b2- And [hence] qad~a , (S, M, A, L,) inf. n. qad~N , (M, L, K,) (tropical:) He clave, cut through by journeying, or passed through, the desert, (S, M, A, O, L, K,) and the night. (M, L) ― -b3- And qad~a bihi AlT~ariyqu , (so in a copy of the M,) or qad~atohu AlT~ariyqu , (so in the L and TA,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (M, L, TA,) i. q. qaTaEahu (M) or qaTaEatohu (L, TA) (tropical:) [ The road cut him off, app. from his companions, or from the object of his journey: compare qaTaEa bihi and quTiEa bihi ]. ― -b4- And qad~a AlkalaAma , (M, L,) inf. n. as above, (M, L, K,) i. q. qaTaEahu (M, L, K *) and $aq~ahu (M, L) [both of which explanations may here mean, as qaTaEa AlkalaAma generally does, (assumed tropical:) He cut short, or broke off, the speech; or ceased from speaking: or both may here mean, as qaTaEa AlkalaAma sometimes does, he articulated speech, or the speech: compare this latter rendering with an explanation of $aq~aqa AlkalaAma ]. ― -b5- [ qad~ahu also signifies He cut it out, or shaped it, in any manner, whether lengthwise or otherwise; like qat~ahu : see this latter, and a verse cited as an ex. of its inf. n.: and see also a saying near the end of the first paragraph of art. frY . Hence] qud~a fulaAnN qad~a Als~ayofi [ Such a one was shaped with the shaping of the sword ] means (tropical:) such a one was made goodly, or beautiful, in respect of Alt~aqoTiyE [i. e. conformation, or proportion, &c., like as is the sword ]. (S, O, L, TA.) [See also qad~N , below.] ― -b6- And qud~ means also (assumed tropical:) He suffered a pain [app. what may be termed a cutting pain ] in the belly, called qudaAd . (M, L, K.)

(Mughnee, K.) ― -b2- (I) It is a noun syn. with Hasobu ; (S, O, Mughnee, K;) generally used indeclinably; (Mughnee, K;) thus accord. to the Basrees; with the d quiescent; (TA;) because resembling qado the particle in respect of the letters composing it, and many other particles in respect of its form, (Mughnee, TA,) such as Eano and balo &c.: (TA:) one says, qado zayodK dirohamN [ The sufficiency of Zeyd (i. e. what is sufficient for Zeyd ) is a dirhem ], (Mughnee, K,) with the d quiescent; (Mughnee, * K, * TA;) and qadiY (S, O) and qadoniY (S, O, Mughnee) [both] meaning HasobiY [ My sufficiency (i. e. what is sufficient for me )]; (S, O;) the n in qadoniY being inserted in order to preserve the quiescence [of the final letter of the noun] because this is the original characteristic of what they make indeclinable; (Mughnee;) but the insertion of the n in this case is anomalous, for it is [by rule] only added in verbs, by way of precaution, [to prevent the confusion of the pronominal affix of the verb and that of the noun,] as in DarabaniY : (S, O:) [see, however, in the next sentence, an explanation of qadoniY accord. to which the n is inserted regularly:] accord. to Yaakoob, using qado in the sense of Hasobu , one says, maA laka EinodiY A_il~aA h`*aA faqado i. e. faqaTo [ There is nothing for thee with me, or nothing due to thee in my possession, except this, and it is a thing sufficient, or it is enough, faqaTo being held to signify properly faHasobu , but it is commonly used as meaning and no more ]; and he asserts it [i. e. qado ] to be a substitute [for qaTo ]: (M:) and it is also used declinably; (Mughnee, K;) thus accord. to the Koofees; (TA;) but this is rare: (Mughnee:) one says qadu zayodK , making it marfooa, (Mughnee, K,) like as one says Hasobuhu ; and qadiY without n [as mentioned above,] like as one says HasobiY . (Mughnee.) ― -b3- (2) It is also a verbal noun, syn. with yakofiY : one says, qado zayodFA dirohamN [ A dirhem suffices, or will suffice, Zeyd ], and qadoniY dirohamN [ A dirhem suffices, or will suffice, me ]; (Mughnee, K;) like as one says yakofiY zayodFA dirohamN , and yakofiyoniY dirohamN . (Mughnee, K. *) -A2- As a particle, it is used peculiarly with a verb, (Mughnee, K,) [i. e.] as such it is not preposed to anything except a verb, (S, O,) either a pret. or an aor., (TA,) from which it is not separated unless by an oath, (Mughnee,) such as is perfectly inflected, enunciative, (Mughnee, K,) not an imperative, (TA,) affirmative, and free from anything that would render it mejzoom or man- soob, and from what is termed Harof tanofiys [i. e. sawofu and its variants]: and it has six meanings. (Mughnee, K.) ― -b2- (1) It denotes expectation: (M, Mughnee, K:) and when it is with an aor., this is evident; (Mughnee;) one says qado yaqodamu AlgaAy^ibu , (Mughnee, K,) meaning It is expected that the absent will come: (TA:) and most affirm that it is thus used with a pret.: (Mughnee:) accord. to some, (M,) it is used in reply to the saying lam~aA yafoEalo [i. e. “ He has not yet done ” such a thing, which implies expectation that he would do it]; (S, M, O;) the reply being, qadofaEala [ Already he has done the thing]: (M:) and Kh asserts that it is used in reply to persons expecting information; (S, M, * O, Mughnee;) [for to such] you say, qado maAta falaAnN [ Already such a one has died ]; but if one inform him who does not expect it, he does not say thus, but he says [merely] maAta fulaAnN : (S, O:) thus some say qado rakiba AlA^amiyru [ Already the commander has mounted his horse] to him who expects his mounting: some, however, disallow that qado is used to denote expectation with the pret. because the pret. denotes what is already past; and hence it appears that those who affirm it to be so used mean that the pret. denotes what was expected before the information: (Mughnee: [in which it is added, with some other observations, that, in the opinion of its author, it does not denote expectation even with the aor.; because the saying yaqodamu Algay^ibu denotes expectation without qado :]) MF says, What we have been orally taught by the sheykhs in ElAndalus is this, that it is a particle denoting the affirmation of truth, or certainty, when it occurs before a pret., and a particle denoting expectation when it occurs before a future. (TA.) ― -b3- (2) It denotes the nearness of the past to the present: (O, Mughnee, K:) so in the saying qado qaAma zayodN [ Zeyd has just, or just now, stood; a meaning often intended by saying merely, has stood ]; (Mughnee, K;) for this phrase without qd may mean the near past and the remote past; (Mughnee;) and so in the saying of the muëdhdhin, qado qaAmati AlS~alaApu [ The time of the rising to prayer has just come, or simply has come ]: (O:) [and, when thus used, it is often immediately preceded by the pret. or aor. of the verb kaAna ; thus you say, kaAna qado *ahaba He had just, or simply had, gone away; and yakuwnu qado *ahaba He will, or shall, have just, or simply have gone away: ] and accord. to the Basrees, except Akh, it must be either expressed or understood immediately before a pret. used as a denotative of state; as in [the saying in the Kur ii. 247,] wamaA lanaA A^al~aA nuqaAtilu fiY sabiyli A@ll~`hi waqado A^uxorijonaA mino diyaArinaA waA^abonaAy^inaA [ And what reason have we that we should not fight in the cause of God when we have been expelled from our abodes and our children? ]; and in [the saying in the Kur iv. 92,] A^awo jaAw^uwkumo HaSirato Suduwruhumo A^no yuqaAtiluwkamo [ Or who come to you, their bosoms being contracted so that they are incapable of fighting you, or their bosoms shrinking from fighting you ]; but the Koofees and Akh says that this is not required, because of the frequent occurrence of the pret. as a denotative of state without qado , and [because] the primary rule is that there should be no meaning, or making, anything to be understood, more especially in the case of that which is in frequent use: (Mughnee:) Sb [however] does not allow the use of the pret. as a denotative of state without qado ; and he makes HSrt Sdwrhm to be an imprecation [meaning may their bosoms become contracted ]: (S in art. HSr ; in which art. in the present work see more on this subject:) and the inceptive la is prefixed to it like of the saying, A_in~a zayodFA laqado qaAma [ Verily Zeyd has just stood, or has stood ]; because the primary rule is that it is to be prefixed to the noun, and it is prefixed to the aor. because it resembles the noun, and when the pret. denotes a time near to the present it resembles the aor. and therefore it is allowable to prefix it thereto. (Mughnee.) [See also the two sentences next after what is mentioned below as the sixth meaning.] ― -b4- (3) It denotes rareness, or paucity; (Mughnee, K;) either of the act signified by the verb, (Mughnee,) as in [the saying], qado yaSoduqu Alka*uwbu [ In some few instances the habitual liar speaks truth ]; (Mughnee, K;) or of what is dependent upon that act, as in [the saying in the Kur xxiv. last verse,] qado yaEolamu maA A^anotumo Ealayohi [as though] meaning A^an~a maA humo Ealayohi huwa A^aqal~u maEoluwmaAtihi [so that it should be rendered At least He knoweth that state of conduct and mind to which ye are conforming yourselves ]: but some assert that in these exs. and the like thereof it denotes the affirmation of truth, or certainty; [as will be shown hereafter;] and that the denoting of rareness, or paucity, in the former ex. is not inferred from qado , but from the saying Alka*uwbu yaSoduqN . (Mughnee.) ― -b5- (4) It denotes frequency; (Mughnee, K;) [i. e.] sometimes (S, O) it is used as syn. with rub~amaA [as denoting frequency, as well as with rub~amaA in the contr. sense, mentioned in the next preceding sentence]: (S, M, O:) thus in the saying (S, M, O, Mughnee, K) of the Hudhalee, (M, Mughnee,) or 'Abeed Ibn-El-Abras, (IB, TA,) qado A^atoruku Alqirona muSofar~FA A^anaAmiluhu [ Often I leave the antagonist having his fingers' ends become yellow ]. (S, M, O, Mughnee, K.) ― -b6- (5) It denotes the affirmation of truth, or certainty: thus in [the saying in the Kur xci. 9,] qado A^afolaHa mano zak~aAhaA [ Verily, or certainly, or indeed, or really, he prospereth, or will prosper, who purifieth it; (namely, his soul;) each pret. here occupying the place of a mejzoom aor.]: (Mughnee, K:) and thus accord. to some in [the saying in the Kur xxiv. last verse, of which another explanation has been given above,] qado yaEolamu maA A^anotumo Ealayohi [ Verily, or certainly, &c., He knoweth that state of conduct and mind to which ye are conforming yourselves ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b7- (6) It denotes negation, (Mughnee, K,) accord. to ISd, (Mughnee,) occupying the place of maA , (M,) in the saying, qado kunota fiY xayorK fataEorifahu , (M, Mughnee, K,) with tErf mansoob, [as though meaning Thou wast not in prosperity, that thou shouldst know it, ] (Mughnee, K,) heard from one of the chaste in speech: (M:) but this is strange. (Mughnee.) ― -b8- [When it is used to denote the nearness of the past to the present, as appears to be indicated by the context in the O,] qado may be separated from the verb by an oath; as in qado waA@ll~`hi A^aHosanota [ Thou hast, by God, done well ] and qado laEamoriY bit~u saAhirFA [ I have, by my life, or by my religion, passed the night sleepless ]. (O, Mughnee. [In the latter, this and what here next follows are mentioned before the explanations of the meanings of the particle; probably because the meaning in these cases can hardly be mistaken.]) And the verb may be suppressed after it, (M, * O, Mughnee,) when its meaning is apprehended, (O,) or because of an indication; (Mughnee;) as in the saying of En-Nábighah (M, O, Mughnee) Edh-Dhubyánee, (O,) A^afida Alt~araH~ulu gayora A^an~a rikaAbanaA lam~aA tazulo biriHaAlinaA wakaA^ano qadi [ The time of departure has drawn near, though the camels that we ride have not left with our utensils and apparatus for travelling, but it is as though they had (left)]; meaning kaA^ano qado zaAlato . (M, O, Mughnee.) ― -b9- If you make qado an Aisom [i. e. a subst. or a proper name], you characterize it by teshdeed: therefore you say, katabotu qad~FA HasanapF [ I wrote a beautiful qd ]; and so you do in the case of kaYo and huwa and lawo ; because these words have no indication of what is deficient in them [supposing them to be originally of three radical letters], therefore it is requisite to add to the last letter of each what is of the same kind as it, and this is incorporated into it: but not in the case of A ; for in this case you add ' ; thus if you name a man laA , or maA , and then add at the end of it A , you make it ' ; for you make the second A movent, and A when movent becomes ' : (S, O:) so says J, [and Sgh has followed him in the O,] and such is the opinion of Akh and of a number of the grammarians of El-Basrah [and of El-Koofeh (MF)], and F has quoted this passage in the B and left it uncontradicted: but IB says, (TA,) [and after him F in the K,] this is a mistake: that only is characterized by teshdeed of which the last letter is infirm: you say, for huwa , (IB, K,) used as the name of a man, (IB,) huw~N , (IB, K,) and for lawo you say law~N , and for fiY you say fiY~N ; (IB;) and such is characterized by teshdeed only in order that the word may not be reduced to one letter on account of the quiescence of the infirm letter [which would disappear] with tenween [as it does in damN and yadN &c.]: (K:) but as to qado , if you use it as a name, you say qadN ; (IB, K;) and for mano you say manN , and for Eano you say EanN ; (K;) like yadN (IB, K) and damN &c.: (K:) F, however, [following IB,] is wrong in calling J's statement a mistake; though the rule given by him [and IB] is generally preferred. (MF, TA.)

sourceDefinition: The skin of a lamb or kid: (M, A, L, Msb, K:) or [only] of a kid: (S, O, L:) or, accord. to IDrd, a small skin, but of what kind he does not say: (M, L:) pl. (of pauc., S) A^aqud~N and (of mult., S) qidaAdN (ISk, S, M, L, Msb, K) and [of pauc. also] A^aqid~apN , which is extr. (M, L.) Hence the saying, ↓ fulaAnN maA yaEorifu Alqad~a mina Alqid~i Such a one knows not the skin of a lamb, or kid, from the thong. (A.) And hence, (O, K,) it is said in a prov., (S, M, A, O,) maA yajomalu qad~aka A_ilaY A^adiymika (S, M, A, O, K) What approximates thy skin of a lamb, or kid, to thy hide [of a full-grown beast]? meaning, accord. to Th, (assumed tropical:) what makes the great to be like the little? (M: [or the little to be like the great? ]) or meaning what induces thee to make thy small affair [ appear ] great? (S:) or what approximates thy small [ affair ] to thy great? (O, K:) applied to him who transgresses his proper limit; (M, O, K;) and to him who compares the contemptible with the noble. (O, K.) ― -b2- See also qid~N , in two places. -A2- Also (assumed tropical:) The measure, quantity, size, or bulk, (M, L, Msb, K,) of a thing: (M, L:) (tropical:) the conformation, or proportion, syn. taqoTiyE , (S, M, A, O, L, K,) of a thing, (M, L,) or of a young woman, (A,) or of a man: (K:) (tropical:) the stature, syn. qaAmap , (S, A, O, L, K,) of a man: (K:) (assumed tropical:) his justness of form, or symmetry: (M, L, K:) and (assumed tropical:) his figure, person, or whole body: (M, L:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aqud~N (M, L, K) and A^aqid~apN , (K,) which is extr., (TA,) and [of mult.] quduwdN (M, L, K) and qidaAdN . (K.) And jaAriyapN Hasanapu Alqad~i (tropical:) A young woman goodly, or beautiful, in respect of stature, and of conformation, or proportion. (A.) And gulaAmN Hasanu Alqad~i (assumed tropical:) A young man goodly, or beautiful, in respect of justness of form, or symmetry, and in person, or the whole of his body. (M, L.) -A3- See, again, qid~N . -A4- By the phrase yaA wayola qad~K , addressed to Mikdád, in a verse of Jereer, is meant yaA wayola miqodaAdK [ O, woe to thee Mikdád ]; the poet restricting himself to some of the letters [of the name]: an instance [more obviously] of a similar kind is sal~aAm used by El- Hoteiäh for sulayomaAn . (O.)

definition: A thing that is maqoduwd [i.
sourceDefinition: A thing that is maqoduwd [i. e. cut in an elongated form, &c.]. (M, L.) ― -b2- [And hence] A thong cut from an untanned skin, (S, M, * A, O, * L, Msb, K,) with which sandals or shoes are sewed, (M, * L, Msb,) and with which a captive is bound; (A;) pl. A^aqud~N : (S, O, L:) and [as a coll. gen. n.] thongs, cut from an untanned skin, with which camels' saddles and [ the vehicles called ] maHaAmil are bound: (M, L:) and ↓ qid~apN [of which the pl. is qidadN ] is a more special term, (S, O, L,) signifying a single thong of this kind. (K.) See an ex. voce qad~N . ― -b3- And (hence, L) A whip; (O, L, K;) as also ↓ qad~N . (K.) Thus in the trad., laqaAbu qawosi A^aHadikumo wamawoDiEu qid~ihi fiY Aljan~api xayorN mina Ald~unoyaA wamaA fiyhaA , (O, * L,) or ↓ qad~ihi , (K,) i. e. Verily the space that would be occupied by the bow of any one of you, and the place that would be occupied by his whip, in Paradise, are better than the present [ sublunary ] world and what is in it: or qid~h may here have the meaning next following. (L.) ― -b4- A sandal; because cut in an elongated form from the skin: (O, L:) or a sandal not stripped of the hair, in order that it may be more pliant. (IAar, O, L.) ― -b5- And A vessel of skin. (S, O, K.) One says, maA lahu qid~N walaA qiHofN He has not a vessel of skin nor a vessel of wood: (S, O, M:) or a skin nor a fragment of a drinking-cup or bowl. (M.) ― -b6- $adiydu Alqid~i occurs in a trad. as some relate it, meaning Having a strong bowstring: but accord. to others, it is ↓ $adiydu Alqad~i , meaning strong in pulling the bow. (L.)

definition: It (a thing) broke, or became broken.
sourceDefinition: It (a thing) broke, or became broken. (Msb.) Said of a wall, it signifies the same: (T, Msb, TA:) or it became thrown down, pulled down, pulled to pieces, demolished, or destroyed, with violence: (A:) or it fell down: (S:) or it cracked, without falling down; (M, K;) as also AinoqaAD~a [from naqaDa ]; inf. n. [of the former] AinoqiDaADN ; (K;) [and AinoqaADa , inf. n. AinoqiyaADN ;] but if it fall, you say, taqay~aDa , inf. n. taqay~uDN : so says AZ: (TA:) A 'Obeyd and others reckon it a biliteral-radical word, belonging to this art.; (M;) or AZ reckons it as such; (TA;) but Aboo- 'Alee makes it a triliteral-radical, [like its syn. AinoqaAD~a ,] from naqaDa , holding its measure to be AifoEal~a . (M, TA.) ― -b2- It became cut in pieces. (TA.) ― -b3- [And hence,] AnqD~t A^awoSaAluhu (assumed tropical:) His connections became sundered, or separated. (TA.) definition: A [ hollow, or cavity, such as is termed ] nuqorap , [generally meaning such as is small, or not large, or such as is round, ] in a mountain, (T, S, O, Msb, K,) in which water stagnates, (T, S, O, Msb,) i.
sourceDefinition: A [ hollow, or cavity, such as is termed ] nuqorap , [generally meaning such as is small, or not large, or such as is round, ] in a mountain, (T, S, O, Msb, K,) in which water stagnates, (T, S, O, Msb,) i. e. the water of the rain, (Msb,) when a torrent pours down; (TA;) similar to what is termed waqob : (T, TA:) in some instances so large as to be capable of containing a hundred times as much as the contents of the [ leathern water-bag called ] mazaAdap : (Msb:) or a nuqorap in a rock: (A:) and any nuqorap in the ground, or in the body: of the fem. gender: (T, O, TA:) and [therefore] its dim. is ↓ qulayotapN : (O:) pl. qilaAtN . (T, S, O, Msb.) Hence the saying, A^asowadu mino maA='i Alqaloti [ Blacker than the water of the qalot ]. (A, TA.) ― -b2- Also A round hollow, or cavity, which water dropping from the roof of a cavern forms in the course of ages in soft stone or in hard ground. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] qalotu Alv~ariydapi (tropical:) The hollow, or depression, of the mess of crumbled bread moistened with gravy, in which the gravy collects. (S, A, O, TA.) ― -b4- And qalotN signifies (tropical:) Any small hollow, or depression, in a member. (A.) ― -b5- And Alqalotu [alone], (TA,) or qalotu Alt~aroquwapi , (A,) (tropical:) The hollow, or depression, that is between the collar-bone and the neck. (A, * TA.) And qalotu AlEayoni (tropical:) The cavity of the eye. (S, A, O.) And qalotu AlS~udogi (tropical:) [ The depression of the temple. ]. (S, O, TA.) And qalotu AlA_ibohaAmi (tropical:) The hollow that is in the lower part of the thumb. (S, O, TA.) And qlt Alkaf~i [app. signifies the same;] (tropical:) The part that is between the tendon of the thumb [i. e. of the flexor longus pollicis ] and the fore finger; which is the middle part between these two [or between the thumb and the fore finger ]. sourceDefinition: is the inf. n. of qanata , (MA, Msb,) aor. , (Msb,) and signifies The being obedient: (S, M, MA, Mgh, K, TA:) or the being constantly obedient: (IAmb, O, TA:) the former is the primary meaning: and hence, in the Kur [xxxiii. 35], ↓ waA@loqaAnitaAti ↓ waA@loqaAnitiyna [ And the obedient men and the obedient women ]. (S, M, TA.) One says, qanata lil~`hi , (MA,) and qanata A@ll~`ha , (TA,) [but this latter is unusual, the former only being authorized by the Kur-án (in iii. 38 and xxxiii. 31),] meaning He was obedient to God. (MA, TA.) And it is said in the Kur [ii. 110 and xxx. 25], ↓ kul~N lahu qaAnituwna i. e. All are obedient unto Him: but the meaning here is, that the beings in heaven [and earth] are created by the will of God, and that none of them can alter the form in which it is created; the obedience here spoken of being obedience to the will [of God], not the obedience of religious service; some of them being obedient [in this sense], and others being disobedient. (L, TA.) [It is said that] the proper signification of ↓ AlqaAnitu [or the signification that implies all the meanings of the word] is The performer of the command of God. (L, TA.) ― -b2- It signifies also The act of standing; (Mgh, TA;) mentioned by Th, and asserted by him to be the primary meaning. (TA.) And (TA) The standing long. (IAmb, O, TA.) And (TA) The standing in the performance of the divinely-appointed act of prayer. (S, Msb, K, TA.) [See also 4.] Hence, (Mgh, Msb, TA,) it is said in a trad. (S, TA) of the Prophet, as a reply given by him to the question A^aY~u AlS~alaApi A^afoDalu , (TA,) A^afoDalu AlS~alaApi Tuwlu Alqunuwti (S, Mgh, Msb, TA) i. e. [ The most excellent characteristic of the performance of the divinely-appointed act of prayer is ] the long continuance of the standing. (Mgh, * Msb, * TA.) And hence, qunuwtu Alwitori ; (S; [see art. wtr ;]) or [as it is also termed] duEaA='u Alqunuwti , which means The supplication of the standing; (Msb;) for one utters the supplication standing: (TA:) and what is thus termed ( duEaA='u Alqunuwti ) is as follows: Aall~ahum~a A_in~aA nasotaEiynuka wanasotagofiruka wanuw^ominu bika wanatawak~alu Ealayoka wanuvoniY Ealayoka Alxayora walaA nakofuruka wanaxolaEu wanatoruku mano yafojuruka Aall~`hum~a A_iy~aAka naEobudu walaka nuSal~iY wanasojudu waA_ilayoka nasoEaY wanaHofidu narojuw raHomataka wanaxo$aY Ea*aAbaka A_in~a Ea*aAbaka biAlkuf~aAri muloHiqN i. e. O God, verily we beg of Thee aid to be obedient and to forsake disobedience, and we beg of Thee forgiveness of sins, [ and we believe in Thee, and we rely upon Thee, ] and we laud Thee well, and we will not be unthankful to Thee for Thy favour, and we cast off and forsake him who disobeys Thee: [ O God, Thee we worship, and to Thee we perform the divinely-appointed act of prayer, and prostrate ourselves; ] and we are quick in working for Thee and in serving Thee: we hope for Thy mercy, and we dread Thy punishment: verily Thy punishment overtakes the unbelievers; thus this clause is expl. on the authority of Ks: or, as some say, it means, causes others to overtake, or become associated with, the unbelievers. (Mgh. [See also art. lHq .]) It is said of the Prophet, qanata $ahorFA fiY SalaApi AlS~uboHi baEoda Alr~ukuwEi yadoEuw EalaY riEolK wa*akuwaAna [ He stood during a month, in the prayer of daybreak, after (the prayers of) the rukuwE (pl. of rakaEa , q. v.), cursing (the tribes of) Rial and Dhekwán ]. (TA.) ― -b3- Also The act of supplicating [ God ]: (Zj, Mgh, O, Msb, K, TA:) this is the signification [most] commonly known. (Zj, Mgh, O, TA.) And [particularly, accord. to general usage,] The supplicating God [ by addressing Him with the form of words mentioned above as used in what is termed duEaA='u Alqunuwti ], doing so standing. (TA.) ― -b4- And The divinely-appointed act of prayer; syn. SalaApN . (IAmb, O, TA.) ― -b5- And The being silent; (O, Msb, K, TA;) by which is meant (O, * TA) the withholding oneself from talking; (O, * K, TA;) in, or during, [ the prayer called ] AlS~alaAp . (O, * Msb, TA.) Hence, (O, Msb, TA,) accord. to a trad., (O, TA,) the saying in the Kur [ii. 239], waquwmuwA ↓ lil~`hi qaAnitiyna [ And stand ye unto God, in the divinely-appointed act of prayer, refraining from talking ]. (O, Msb, TA.) ― -b6- And The serving of God. (TA.) ― -b7- And The continuing of the performance of the pilgrimage. (TA.) One says, [ qanata and] ↓ Aqnt , meaning He continued the performance of the pilgrimage. (IAar, O, K, TA.) ― -b8- And The prolonging of engaging in warring, or warring and plundering. (TA.) One says, [ qanata and] ↓ Aqnt , meaning He prolonged the engaging in warring, or warring and plundering. (IAar, O, K, TA.) ― -b9- And The confessing, or acknowledging, one's being in the condition of a servant [ to God ]. (TA.) ― -b10- And The being lowly, humble, or submissive: (A, TA:) or the keeping to obedience [ to God ], with lowliness, humility, or submissiveness. (Er-Rághib, TA.) One says, qanata lahu He was, or became, lowly, humble, or submissive, to him. (TA.) And qanatati AlmrAp lizawojihaA , (A,) or libaEolihaA , (TA,) The woman was, or became, lowly, humble, or submissive, and obedient, to her husband: (A:) or was, or became, quiet and submissive; syn. A^aqar~at . (TA.) [See also 4, and 8.] -A2- qanaAtapN [is an inf. n., of which the verb is qanuta , like qatuna , and] signifies The eating little [like qataAnapN ]. (K.)

sourceDefinition: [ A shackle; or fetter: or, generally, a pair of shackles for the fore-legs of a beast, and generally made of rope, but some are of iron; a pair of hobbles; a pair of fetters ]: (S, K, &c.:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aqoyaAdN (L, Msb, K) and [of mult.] quyuwdN . (S, L, Msb, K.) ― -b2- A_in~ quyuwda AlA^ayaAdo A^awovaqu AlA^aqoyaAdo (tropical:) [ Verily the shackles of benefactions are the firmest of shackles ]. (A.) [ AlA^ayaAdo is for AlA^ayaAdiY .] ― -b3- What binds together [ the two pieces of wood in a camel's saddle which are called ] the EaDudaAni of [ the two broad pieces of wood called ] the muw^ax~arataAni , (L, K [in the former of which, however, instead of mA Dm~ AlEDdyn mn Almwx~rtyn , the reading in the K, is put mA Dm~ AlEDdtyn Almw^x~rtyn , which I suppose to be a mistake]) at their upper part, being a thong. (L.) ― -b4- A plaited thong between [ the two pieces of wood called ] the HinowaAni of a camel's saddle of the kind called raHol , at the upper part; and sometimes, of a horse's saddle. (L.) ― -b5- The thong that binds together [ the two pieces of wood called ] the EaroquwataAni of a camel's saddle of the kind called qatab . (S, L, K.) ― -b6- Anything that binds one part of a thing to another part. (L.) ― -b7- The extended thing at the lower extremities of the suspensory cords or strings of a sword, which is held by [ the rings called ] the bakaraAt . (L, K.) ― -b8- qayodaA AlbaAziY The jesses of the hawk or falcon; syn. sibaAqaAhu (S, O, K, all in art. sbq .) ― -b9- qayodu AlA^asonaAni The gum wherein the teeth are set: (K:) quyuwdu AlAsnAn the gums: (L:) or the portions of the flesh of the gums that rise between the teeth; likened to the red quyuwd which are marks upon camels, made with a hot iron. (ISd, L.) ― -b10- qayodu Alfarasi A certain mark made with a hot iron upon the neck of a camel, (S, ISd, L, K,) and upon its face, and thigh, of an oblong shape, (ISd, L,) in the form of a qayod [ for the legs ], (S, L,) or of two rings with a line extending between them. (Nh, L.) ― -b11- qayodu AlA^awaAbidi (tropical:) [lit. Shackles upon the legs of the wild animals which shun, and take fright at, mankind &c.; or, accord. to the L, of the wild asses ]: indeterminate in signification, though determinate in its grammatical form: (Sb, L:) an appellation given to a horse, (K,) or to a fleet, or swift, and excellent horse, because, by its swiftness, it overtakes the wild beasts, (T, K,) and prevents their escaping. (T, S.) qyd is here a proper subst. used as an epithet because it imports the attribute of a verb; or it is for taqoyid . (IJ, L.) [See also art. Abd and Ham, p. 455.] ― -b12- (tropical:) A wife: as also gul~N . (TA.) ― -b13- maA EalaY h`*aA AlHarofi qyado (tropical:) There is not upon this letter a syllabical sign, or sign which points out the pronunciation, or the division of syllables. (A.) ― -b14- Alqayodu waAlr~atoEapu , a prov.: see art. rtE . -A2- See also qiydN .

definition: The place of the qayod in the leg of a horse;
sourceDefinition: The place of the qayod in the leg of a horse; (S, K;) [i. e., the pastern ]. Ex. farasN Eabolu Almuqay~adi Tawiylu Almuqal~adi [ A horse large in the place of the shackle, or pastern; long in the place of the collar, or neck ]. (A.) ― -b2- The place of the anklet in [ the leg of ] a woman; (S, K;) [i. e., the ankle ]. ― -b3- muqay~adN [and ↓ maqiydN ] A camel, or the like, having his legs shackled; having shackles upon his legs: pl. [of the latter] maqaAyiydu . (K.) You say h`w^ulaA='i A^ajomaAlN maqaAyiydN , i. e., muqay~adaAtN` [ These are camels having their legs shackled ]. Hence applied to a place abounding with herbage, or pasture. (L.)

definition: lx~Shu , (A, TA,) inf.
sourceDefinition: lx~Shu , (A, TA,) inf. n. taloxiySN , (S, A, K,) He explained, expounded, or interpreted, it; (S, A, K;) he made it clear; (A, K;) namely, language: (A:) taloxiySN and taboyiynN and $aroHN and taxoliySN all signify the same: (A:) he went to the utmost point in explaining it, expounding it, interpreting it, and making it plain: namely, a thing; as also lH~Shu . (TA.) You say, lax~iSo liY xabaraka Explain thou to me thy news, or information, thing after thing. (TA.) (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yaluwtu , He told, narrated, or gave an account of, a thing different from that respecting which he was asked. (K.) [But accord. to some, the aor. is yaliytu , and the verb belongs to art. lyt .] It was said to ElAsadeeyeh, “ What is AlmudaAHalapu ” and she answered A^ano yaliyta AlA_inosaAnu $ayoy^FA qado Ealimahu , i. e., “ The concealing a thing that one knows, and telling, or narrating, something different from it. ” (TA.) ― -b2- laAta Alxabara , aor. yaluwtu , He concealed the news, or information, (K,) and related what was different therefrom. (TA.) [But see above.] ― -b3- laAta Alr~ajula , aor. yaluwtu , He told the man, or narrated to him, a thing in a manner different from the real state of the case: or he expressed the news, or information, to him obscurely, or enigmatically, or obscured it to him, or concealed it from him, telling him, narrating to him, or giving him an account of, a thing different from that respecting which he was asked: but accord. to As., laAtahu , aor. yaliytuhu , [not yaluwtuhu .] inf. n. layotN , signifies “ he expressed to him the news, or information, obscurely, or enigmatically, or obscured it to him, or concealed it from him ”: thus he makes it belong to art. lyt : and the like is said in the L. See also above. (TA.) ― -b4- laAtahu , aor. yaluwtu ; as also laAtahu , aor. yaliytu ; He withheld him, or restrained him, and turned him, or averted him, from his course, purpose, or object. (S, K, art lyt , q. v.)

sourceDefinition: , (K,) inf. n. mulaAwaSapN , (M,) He looked to the right and left as though he desired, or sought, a thing: (M:) or he looked as though he were deceiving, or beguiling, to seek to obtain, or attain, a thing; (Lth, K;) as also ↓ laASa , inf. n. lawoSN . (Lth.) -A2- lAwShu biEayonihi , (M, TA,) inf. n. as above, (M, A, K,) He looked, (M,) or glanced, (A, K,) at him, or it, from the interstice of a door, (M, A, K,) and the like, (A, K,) or of a curtain; (M;) as also ↓ laASahu , (M,) inf. n. lawoSN : (M, A, K:) or the former verb has the signification here first given. (M.) ― -b2- lAwS Al$~ajara He looked (S, A, K) to the right and left (A, K) to see how he might come to the trees, (S, K,) to pull them up, or out, (S,) or to cut them with the axe, and to see how he might strike them, (K,) or to see how he might cut them. (A.) ― -b3- And hence, laAwaSaniY fulaAnu Eano ka*aA Such a one endeavoured to turn me by deceit, or guile, from such a thing. (A.) [Hence also,] maA zilotu A^ulaAwiSuhu Eano ka*aA , (M,) and Eanohu ↓ A^uliySuhu , (M, TA,) I ceased not to endeavour to turn him from such a thing; i. e. to endeavour to induce him to leave, or relinquish, such a thing; syn. A^udyruhu Eanohu : (M, TA:) and EalaY ka*aA ↓ A^ulaASahu , (S, K,) and laAwaSahu Ealayohi , (M, K, art. dwr ,) he endeavoured to turn him to, or induce him to do, such a thing, ( A^adaArahu Ealayohi ,) desiring, or seeking, it of him. sourceDefinition: What is in the belly of a pregnant animal, (IAar, Mgh,) or of a she-camel, (Msb, K,) and of a ewe or a she-goat, (K,) when her pregnancy has become manifest: (TA:) or (Msb; in the K, and) the sale of a thing for what is in the belly of a certain she-camel: (S, Msb:) or the sale of a camel, or other thing, for what is in the belly of a she-camel: (AZ, Mgh, * TA:) or the purchase of what is in the bellies of she-camels and of ewes or she-goats: and the purchase of a camel for what is in the belly of a she-camel: and ↓ majarN [signifies the same, but] is a word of weak authority, or a barbarism; (K:) and the latter appears to be the case, for it is rejected by Az and IAth: (TA:) or (Msb; in the K, and) i. q. muHaAqalapN [or the sale of corn in the ear for wheat-grain ]: (IAar, Msb, K:) and muzaAbanapN [or the sale of dates on the tree for dates by measure ]: and (assumed tropical:) a game of hazard; syn. qimaArN : and (assumed tropical:) usury; syn. ribFY : (IAar, K:) it is a subst. from A^amojara fiY AlbayoEi . (Msb.) majorN , (S,) or bayoEu Almajori , (TA,) is forbidden in a trad. (S, TA.) Perhaps bayoEu Almajori may be termed mjr in this trad. tropically. (TA.) -A2- A great army (see a verse cited in art. dhm ).

sourceDefinition: [a coll. gen. n.] Pieces, or bits, [or lumps, or clods, ] of dry, or tough, clay, (M, A, K,) such as is cohesive: (TA:) or [simply] pieces of clay: (Az, Msb:) or compact or cohesive earth: (Msb:) or tough or cohesive clay in which is no sand: (M, Msb, K:) n. un. with p . (S, M, Msb, K.) In the expression ↓ AlHijaArapu waAlmidaArapu [ Stones and pieces of dry or tough clay, &c.], the latter word is used after the manner of an imitative sequent, and is not used alone, as a broken pl.: (M:) or it is an imitative sequent. (K.) -A2- (tropical:) Cities [or towns or villages ]: or a region, district, or tract, of cities or towns or villages, and of cultivated land; (K, TA;) because its buildings are [generally] of madar : (TA:) and its n. un., ↓ madarapN , (tropical:) a city or town or village; syn. balodapN , (K,) or qaroyapN ; (S, Msb, K;) because its buildings are generally of madar : (Msb:) or a town or village built of clay or mud and unburnt bricks: and also a large city. (L.) You say, A^aholu Almadari waAlwabari (tropical:) [ The people of the towns or villages, and of the tents ]. (S.) And maA raA^ayotu fiY Alwabari waAlmadari mivolahu (tropical:) I have not seen in the desert and the towns or villages the like of him. (A.) And it is related in a trad., that the Prophet said to 'Ámir Ibn-Et-Tufeyl, Become thou a muslim, and he replied, EalaY A^an~a liYa Alwabara walaka Almadara (tropical:) [ On the condition that to me shall pertain the desert, and to thee the towns or villages ]. (A.) You say also, fulaAnN say~idu madaratihi (tropical:) Such a one is the chief of his town or village. (Msb.) And ↓ banuw madoraA='a (tropical:) The people of the cities or towns or villages and cultivated land. (K.)

definition: What is sucked from, or of, a thing;
sourceDefinition: What is sucked from, or of, a thing; (M, TA;) as also ↓ muSaASapN . (M, A, TA.) You say, TaAbato muSaASatuhu fiY famiY What was sucked from it, or of it, was good, or sweet, or pleasant, in my mouth. (A.) ― -b2- [And hence,] The pure, or choice, part of anything; (S, K;) as also ↓ muSaAmiSN : (K:) and (S) the purest, or choicest, (S, M,) of a thing; as also ↓ muSaASapN and ↓ muSaAmiSN . (M.) And AlmaAli ↓ muS~apu signifies the same as muSaASuhu , (K, TA,) i. e. The pure, or choice part of property, or of the property. (TA.) You say, fulaAnN muSaASu qawomihi , (S, M,) and ↓ muSaASatuhu , (M,) Such a one is the purest in race, or lineage, of his people: and in like manner you say of two, and of more, and of a female. (S, M.) And huwa mino muSaASi qawomihi [ He is of the purest, or choicest, of his people ]. (A.) ― -b3- Also, Pure, or choice, applied to Hasab [or grounds of pretension to respect, &c.]; as also ↓ muSaAmiSN . (A.) You say also, A_in~ahu lamuSaAmiSN fiY qawomihi Verily he is distinguished, or characterized, by pure grounds of respect among his people. (K, * TA.) ― -b4- Also, The origin, source, or place of origination, of a thing. (M, TA.) You say, huwa kariymu AlmuSaASi He is generous, or noble, in respect of origin. (TA.) Accord. to Lth, muSaASu Alqawomi signifies The original source of the people: and the most excellent of their middle class. (TA.)

(M.) ― -b2- A man who sucks his ewes or she-goats; by reason of his meanness, or ungenerousness: (A'Obeyd, S, K:) i. e. who sucks from their udders with his mouth; lest the sound of the milking should be heard; as also, ↓ maAS~u ; (TA;) and so maloHaAnu and mak~aAnu . (TA) of the baZor [q. v.], (K, TA,) of thy mother: (S, K, TA:) or the meaning is O sucker ( raADiE ) of the ewes or she-goats: (K:) ISk says, (TA,) you should not say ↓ yaA maAS~aAnu : (S, TA:) but Ibn-'Abbád says, (TA,) one says wayoliY EalaY maAS~aAni boni maAS~aAnK , and ↓ maAS~aAnapa boni maAS~aAnapa , (K, TA,) meaning [ Alas for me, on account of ] the mean, or ungenerous, the son of the mean, or ungenerous! (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yamiydu , inf. n. mayodN (S, L, Msb, K) and mayadaAnN , (L, Msb, K,) It (a thing) was, or became in a state of motion, or commotion; was, or became agitated: (S, L, Msb, K:) or, in a state of violent motion or commotion; or violently agitated. (El-Basáïr, TA.) So in the expression in the Kur, [xvi. 15; and xxxi. 9;] A^ano tamiyda bikumo Lest it (the earth) should be convulsed with you, and go round with you, and move you about violently. (El-Basáïr, TA.) ― -b2- maAda It turned or twisted about, or became contorted and convulsed. (IKtt.) ― -b3- maAda fiY Alr~umoHi (tropical:) He (a man pierced) writhed upon the spear. (A.) ― -b4- maAda It (the mirage, saraAb ,) was in a state of commotion; it quivered, or trembled. (L, K.) ― -b5- maAda (assumed tropical:) He was, or became, confounded, perplexed, or amazed. (TA.) ― -b6- maAda , (aor. yamiydu , TA, inf. n. mayodN or mayadN , L,) (tropical:) He (a man, L,) became affected with a heaving of the stomach, or a tendency to vomit, and a giddiness in the head, by reason of intoxication, or of voyaging upon the sea. (L, K.) ― -b7- You say also maAda bihi AlbaHoru , aor. yamiydu , inf. n. mayodN , (tropical:) The sea affected him with a heaving of the stomach, &c. (L.) And maAdato bihi AlA^aroDu (tropical:) The ground went round with him. (A.) ― -b8- maAdati AlHanoZalapu , (aor. yamiydu , L,) The colocynth became affected by day-dew, (L, K,) or by moisture, (L,) and in consequence, changed [ in odour, or stinking ]: (L, K:) and in like manner a date. (L.) ― -b9- maAda , (S, A, L,) inf. n. mayodN (L) and mayadaAnN ; (A;) and ↓ tmAyd ; (A;) It (a branch) inclined from side to side. (S, A, L.) ― -b10- (tropical:) He inclined from side to side in walking. (L.) ― -b11- maAda , inf. n. mayodN and mayadaAnN , It inclined to one side: as the earth is, in a trad., described to have done before the mountains were formed. (L.) ― -b12- maAda (tropical:) He (a man, S,) affected a bending of his person, body, or limbs; (L;) he walked with an elegant and a proud and self-conceited gait, with an affected inclining of his body from side to side; (S, L, K;) and maAdato and ↓ tmy~dt signify the same, said of a woman. (A.) -A2- maAda He conferred, or bestowed, a benefit or benefits, or a favour or favours. You say, maAdaniY fulaAnN Such a one conferred a benefit or benefits upon me. (L.) ― -b2- maAdah , (L, Msb,) and ↓ AmAdhu , (L,) He gave him. (L, Msb.) ― -b3- maAda He furnished persons with, or gave them, provisions for travelling; syn. zaAda . (L.) [In the K, zaAra He visited. ] ― -b4- He brought a people wheat, or food; i. q. maAra , (S, L, K,) of which it is a dial. form. (S.) ― -b5- He trafficked as a merchant. (L.) ― -b6- maAda , inf. n. mayodN and mayadaAnN , It increased, or grew; syn. raAEa and zakaA . (M, L, K.) [In the copies of the K in my hands, for rAE is put zAg .]

sourceDefinition: (S, L, Msb, K, &c.) and ↓ miydaAnN (K) A horse-course; race-ground; hippodrome: (Msb, TA:) pl. mayaAdiynu : (S, K, &c.:) of the measure faEolaAnN , (IKtt,) from mAd “ it was in a state of motion; ” because the sides of the horsecourse shake on the occasion of a race: (Msb:) or from mAd “ it turned or twisted about, or became contorted and convulsed; ” because the horses wheel about, and bend or convulse themselves, in the place so called: or of the measure faloEaAnN , from madFY “ a limit, or goal; ” because horses run to their goals in the place so called; originally madoyaAnN , the second and third radicals being transposed; as in biyzaAnN , originally buzoyaAnN : or of the measure fayoEaAlN , from madana “ he abode, or dwelt; ” because horses confine themselves especially to the place so called for wheeling about and the like. (S, L.) ― -b2- mayodaAnu AlxulafaA='i (tropical:) a term applied by historians to The period of the reign of Khaleefehs; from twenty to twenty-four years. (MF, TA.)

sourceDefinition: (and ↓ mayodapN , El-Jarmee, L, K) A table with food upon it: (S, L, K:) without food upon it, a table is not thus called, but is called xiwaAnN : (AAF, S, L:) or also applied to a table itself: (L:) MF says, that this latter application is allowable, considering that food has been, or is to be, placed upon the table: but El-Hareeree asserts it to be incorrect, and the former application only to be allowable: (TA:) mAy^dp is thus used in its proper sense of an act. part. n., and is from mAd “ it was in a state of motion; ” as though the table [which was generally a round piece of leather or the like spread upon the ground] moved about with what was upon it: (Zj, L, Msb: *) or from mAd “ he brought wheat or food; ” because food is brought upon it [or as though it brought food]: (L:) or from mAd “ he gave; ” as though it gave of what was upon it to those around it: (El-'Ináyeh:) or it is of the form of an act. part. n. and used in the sense of a pass. part. n., from mAd “ he gave, ” (AO, S, L, Msb,) like raADiyapN in the phrase Eiy$apN raADiyapN ; (AO, S, L;) because what is thus called is given by its owner to the people [who are to eat]: (Msb:) also, food itself; (Akh, AHát, ISd, L, K;) even if without a table: (L:) [pl. mawaAy^idu ]. See also faAvuwrN . ― -b2- maAy^idapN : (tropical:) A round piece of land or ground: (L, K:) likened to a table. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. naHiyHN , He (a man) reiterated a sound, or made it to reciprocate, ( rad~adahu ,) in his inside: (S, L:) or his voice was reiterated, or made to reciprocate, ( tarad~ada ,) in his inside; as also ↓ naHonaHa and ↓ tanaHonaHa : (K:) [each of these verbs, of which the last seems to be the most common, signifies, as is implied in the L &c., and accord. to present usage, he made a reiterated humming in his throat, like a slight coughing, or, as some say, more violent than coughing; as is often done by a niggard when he is asked for a thing:] Alt~anaHonuHu is well known, (S,) and Aln~aHonaHapu is like it; (Lth, S;) it is [ the making a sound, or sounds, in the throat, ] slighter than coughing; and is the pretence of the niggard: (Lth:) or it is more violent than coughing; as also Aln~aHiyHu . (L.) See also Hir~apN . ― -b2- [Hence, from the sound employed,] naH~a , aor. , He incited, or urged on, a camel. (K.)
